title: Study of GeSn Selective Area Growth with Demonstration of SWIR Light Detection
summary: As germanium-tin (GeSn) epitaxial growth quality continuously improves, the search for an efficient integration strategy of GeSn optoelectronics devices into complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) manufacturing line also accelerates. Selective area growth (SAG) on patterned substrate emerges as a promising approach for this quest, with locally controlled growth of GeSn laser/detector suitable for either co-integration with silicon-based waveguide structure or stand-alone module like focal plane array. In this work, we report successful GeSn SAG with Sn content ranging from 3.2% to 8.7% of good optical quality, with demonstration of tunable GeSn SAG photoluminescence and GeSn SAG photoconductor device, the latter with detection cutoff wavelength up to 2 um. In addition, we present a comprehensive study of GeSn SAG condition at different window sizes, from 2 um to 100 um, and shapes: circle, square, octagon, and rectangle. Presence of loading effect is revealed, where GeSn growth rate increases as pattern fill factor and window size shrink. It introduces a different growth condition compared to thin film growth, which can weaken or inhibit Sn incorporation at very small window size and induce Sn segregation in high Sn content SAG growth.

AI.tldr: This paper reports successful selective area growth (SAG) of GeSn with Sn content from 3.2% to 8.7%, demonstrating tunable photoluminescence and photoconductor devices with detection cutoff up to 2 µm. It reveals a loading effect where growth rate increases with smaller pattern windows, causing reduced Sn incorporation and potential Sn segregation.
AI.motivation: To develop an efficient integration strategy for GeSn optoelectronics into CMOS manufacturing lines by leveraging selective area growth (SAG) on patterned substrates for co-integration with silicon waveguides or stand-alone modules.
AI.method: GeSn SAG was performed on patterned substrates with varying window sizes (2–100 µm) and shapes (circle, square, octagon, rectangle). Sn content, optical quality, and device performance were characterized via photoluminescence and photoconductor measurements.
AI.result: Successful GeSn SAG with Sn content from 3.2% to 8.7% of good optical quality; photoconductor devices achieved detection cutoff up to 2 µm. A loading effect was observed: growth rate increases as pattern fill factor and window size decrease, which can weaken Sn incorporation at small window sizes and induce Sn segregation at high Sn content.
AI.conclusion: GeSn SAG is a viable approach for CMOS-compatible integration of GeSn optoelectronics, but the loading effect must be carefully controlled to maintain Sn incorporation and avoid segregation, especially at small feature sizes.

title: Quantitative Infrared Thermographic Assessment of Hand Cooling Dynamics During Controlled Contact with Metal Plates
summary: This study investigates the spatiotemporal thermal response of human hands during controlled contact cooling using short wave infrared (SWIR), mid wave infrared (MWIR), and long wave infrared (LWIR) thermography. Three participants simultaneously placed one hand on a cooling metal plate and the contralateral hand on a reference plate maintained near room temperature. Temperature evolution was analyzed in five anatomical regions, including the distal finger, proximal finger, vessel associated region, non vessel region, and forearm. Quantitative metrics, including temperature variation, bilateral temperature difference, initial cooling rate, and frequency-domain amplitude, were extracted from the thermal image sequences. The results showed that the finger regions exhibited the largest temperature reductions and highest cooling rates, indicating greater sensitivity to thermal stimulation than the dorsal hand and forearm. MWIR and LWIR measurements revealed highly consistent cooling dynamics, while LWIR imaging provided enhanced thermal contrast and sensitivity. Frequency-domain analysis demonstrated that the dominant thermal response was concentrated in the low frequency range below 0.05 Hz. Furthermore, pixel-wise cooling rate maps highlighted substantial spatial heterogeneity across the hand surface. Numerical bioheat simulations confirmed that blood perfusion and skin plate contact conductance are key factors governing the cooling response. These findings demonstrate the potential of dynamic infrared thermography as a non-contact tool for assessing peripheral thermoregulation and vascular function during controlled cooling experiments.

AI.tldr: This study uses SWIR, MWIR, and LWIR thermography to analyze hand cooling dynamics during contact with a cold plate, finding that fingers cool fastest, LWIR offers best contrast, thermal responses are below 0.05 Hz, and spatial heterogeneity is significant, with numerical simulations identifying blood perfusion and contact conductance as key factors.
AI.motivation: To investigate the spatiotemporal thermal response of human hands during controlled contact cooling using multiple infrared bands and to assess dynamic infrared thermography as a non-contact tool for evaluating peripheral thermoregulation and vascular function.
AI.method: Three participants placed one hand on a cooled metal plate and the contralateral hand on a room-temperature reference plate. Thermal image sequences were captured using SWIR, MWIR, and LWIR cameras. Temperature evolution was analyzed across five anatomical regions (distal finger, proximal finger, vessel-associated region, non-vessel region, forearm). Metrics included temperature variation, bilateral temperature difference, initial cooling rate, and frequency-domain amplitude. Pixel-wise cooling rate maps were generated, and numerical bioheat simulations were performed.
AI.result: Fingers showed the largest temperature reductions and highest cooling rates. MWIR and LWIR measurements were highly consistent; LWIR provided superior thermal contrast and sensitivity. Dominant thermal response was below 0.05 Hz. Cooling rate maps revealed substantial spatial heterogeneity. Simulations confirmed blood perfusion and skin-plate contact conductance as key governing factors.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic infrared thermography, particularly LWIR, is a promising non-contact method for assessing peripheral thermoregulation and vascular function during controlled cooling.

title: Full-band reciprocal parametric amplification in coupled oscillator arrays
summary: Parametric resonance provides a versatile mechanism to manipulate wave signals in time-modulated metamaterials, but typically operates within narrow wavelength or frequency ranges. Here, we show that one-dimensional arrays of coupled resonators can generically exhibit parametric amplification across an entire band under standing-wave parametric modulation. We develop a general physical framework to describe the parametric resonance of isolated bands, derive modulation conditions needed to achieve band-wide amplification for a given band, and demonstrate their validity in a model of active mechanical metamaterials based on tunable membrane resonator arrays. We numerically demonstrate applications of the proposed strategy in distortion-free amplification and temporal splitting of wave packets, with results in quantitative agreement with our theoretical calculations. Our strategies for broadband amplification can be generalized to other active wave media with nearly flat or cosine-like dispersion relations, with potential applications in loss-mitigation, noise squeezing, and programmable wave manipulation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that 1D arrays of coupled resonators can achieve broadband parametric amplification across an entire band using standing-wave parametric modulation, demonstrated in active mechanical metamaterials with applications in distortion-free amplification and wave packet splitting.
AI.motivation: Parametric resonance in time-modulated metamaterials typically operates only within narrow wavelength or frequency ranges, limiting its utility. The authors aim to overcome this bottleneck by achieving amplification across an entire band.
AI.method: The authors develop a general physical framework for parametric resonance of isolated bands, derive modulation conditions for band-wide amplification, and validate the theory through numerical simulations in a model of active mechanical metamaterials based on tunable membrane resonator arrays.
AI.result: Demonstrated distortion-free amplification and temporal splitting of wave packets with quantitative agreement between numerical and theoretical results. The strategy works for bands with nearly flat or cosine-like dispersion relations.
AI.conclusion: The broadband parametric amplification strategy can be generalized to other active wave media, with potential applications in loss-mitigation, noise squeezing, and programmable wave manipulation.

title: Determination of the roles of strain and tearing in single photon emission from nanoindented WSe$_2$
summary: Single-photon emission in two-dimensional single-layer WSe2 is attractive for the on-demand generation of quantum states of light. The electronic states that are responsible for single-photon generation preferentially form in regions of localized tensile strain, enabling deterministic positioning and strain engineering. Nanoindentation of single-layer WSe2 yields controlled and reproducible deformations that generate the localized strain needed to activate the single-photon-emitting states. However, using nanoindentation both for investigating structure-property relationships and for manufacturing quantum light sources based on WSe2 is hindered by key questions on the structural integrity of the indented 2D material, the resulting strain generated, and the sub-micron location of the emitters. In this work, we study the structure of indented single-layer WSe2 using a fabrication process that inverts the indents into protruding pillars that can be probed using electron microscopy. We explicitly identify strain relaxation of the indented single-layer WSe2 due to tearing and confirm that single-photon-emitting states still form in these systems, likely at the extremities of the tear. For indents that are confirmed to be intact (i.e., not torn), we assess the ability to strain engineer the single-photon emitters. While strain does not strongly affect the emission energy or the brightness, we find that increased strain reduces the spatial density of emitters. This trend indicates that an optimal amount of strain is needed for emitter formation and/or the emitters preferentially form on the periphery of the indent. Our investigation provides insight into the most relevant structure-property relationships for using strain to engineer quantum light sources in single-layer WSe2 and other 2D semiconductors.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the structural integrity and strain effects of nanoindented single-layer WSe2 for single-photon emission. It reveals that indented WSe2 can undergo strain relaxation via tearing, yet emitters still form at tear extremities. For intact indents, increased strain reduces emitter spatial density without strongly affecting emission energy or brightness, suggesting an optimal strain range for emitter formation.
AI.motivation: To resolve key questions about the structural integrity, strain generation, and sub-micron location of single-photon emitters in nanoindented single-layer WSe2, which currently hinder both fundamental structure-property studies and the manufacturing of quantum light sources.
AI.method: The authors developed a fabrication process that inverts indents into protruding pillars for electron microscopy analysis, enabling direct structural characterization of indented single-layer WSe2. They compared torn (strain-relaxed) and intact indents, and systematically studied the influence of strain on emission energy, brightness, and spatial density of single-photon emitters.
AI.result: Strain relaxation via tearing was explicitly identified in indented WSe2, yet single-photon emitters still formed, likely at tear extremities. For intact indents, increased strain did not strongly affect emission energy or brightness but significantly reduced the spatial density of emitters.
AI.conclusion: An optimal amount of strain is needed for emitter formation, and/or emitters preferentially form on the periphery of the indent. These findings provide key structure-property relationships for strain engineering of quantum light sources in single-layer WSe2 and other 2D semiconductors.

title: Eddy currents and current reversal in curved magnetic thin-film Josephson junctions
summary: Real-space geometric curvature in magnetic thin films introduces a controllable mechanism for tailoring the pathways of superconducting steady-state Josephson currents via the proximity effect. We present a generalized Green's function method for calculating diffusive transport in arbitrarily curved surfaces, and show how the competing mechanisms of curvature and distance regulate conversion between different superconducting pairings in a proximity-coupled ferromagnet. We show how this dictates the distribution of current density, with the possibility of curvature-controlled current density manipulation, induced eddy currents and current reversal.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a generalized Green's function method to study how geometric curvature in magnetic thin films controls superconducting Josephson currents via the proximity effect, revealing curvature-induced manipulation of current density, eddy currents, and current reversal.
AI.motivation: To introduce a controllable mechanism (real-space geometric curvature) for tailoring steady-state Josephson currents in superconducting thin films, and to understand how curvature and distance regulate superconducting pairing conversions in proximity-coupled ferromagnets.
AI.method: A generalized Green's function method for calculating diffusive transport in arbitrarily curved surfaces is developed, incorporating the proximity effect and competing curvature-distance mechanisms.
AI.result: Curvature dictates the distribution of current density, enabling curvature-controlled current density manipulation, induced eddy currents, and current reversal.
AI.conclusion: Geometric curvature provides a controllable pathway for tailoring superconducting currents in magnetic thin films, offering new possibilities for current manipulation in hybrid superconductor-ferromagnet systems.

title: Multibath Influence Matrices: Universal Scaling from Real-Time Dynamics
summary: Diverging timescales are the hallmark of critical dynamics and the bottleneck to their classical and quantum simulation. To tame this, we compress a spacetime tensor network: temporally into semigroup influence matrices and spatially via matrix-product states. Benchmarking on the two-impurity Anderson model with its four fermionic species, we compute spectral functions to map the evolution from a Kondo resonance, across a non-Fermi-liquid quantum critical point, and into a gapped singlet phase. Resolving transient through asymptotic dynamics in sudden quenches and Kibble-Zurek ramps, we obtain the universal two-channel-Kondo exponent. Together, these results establish multibath influence matrices as a practical tool for real-time dynamics in strongly correlated multi-orbital systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a spacetime tensor network compression technique using semigroup influence matrices (temporal) and matrix-product states (spatial) to simulate critical dynamics with diverging timescales. Benchmarking on the two-impurity Anderson model, they compute spectral functions across a quantum critical point, resolve transient and asymptotic dynamics, and extract the universal two-channel-Kondo exponent, establishing multibath influence matrices as a practical tool for real-time dynamics in strongly correlated multi-orbital systems.
AI.motivation: Diverging timescales are the hallmark of critical dynamics and the bottleneck to classical and quantum simulation; the authors aim to tame this computational challenge.
AI.method: Compress a spacetime tensor network: temporally into semigroup influence matrices and spatially via matrix-product states.
AI.result: Computed spectral functions mapping the evolution from a Kondo resonance, across a non-Fermi-liquid quantum critical point, into a gapped singlet phase; resolved transient through asymptotic dynamics in sudden quenches and Kibble-Zurek ramps; obtained the universal two-channel-Kondo exponent.
AI.conclusion: Multibath influence matrices are established as a practical tool for real-time dynamics in strongly correlated multi-orbital systems.

title: Gaussian Reformulation of the Feynman Path Integral for Quantum Statistical Mechanics with Results for the Second Virial Coefficient of $^4$He
summary: The Feynman path integral for quantum statistical mechanics is reformulated as Gaussian sampling of the neighborhood of each position configuration. The variance and mean are obtained from ring polymer statistics on a lattice, and from the high temperature expansion of the Wigner-Kirkwood commutation function, respectively. The algorithm avoids multiple temperature nodes for each configuration and the need for numerical cancelation in the statistical averages, which are problematic for conventional path integral quantum Monte Carlo. Analytic and simulation results for the second virial coefficient of helium are compared to laboratory measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates Feynman path integrals for quantum statistical mechanics using Gaussian sampling around each position configuration, with variance from ring polymer lattice statistics and mean from high-temperature Wigner-Kirkwood expansion. This avoids multiple temperature nodes and numerical cancellation issues in conventional path integral quantum Monte Carlo. Results for helium's second virial coefficient match laboratory measurements.
AI.motivation: To overcome problems in conventional path integral quantum Monte Carlo methods, specifically the need for multiple temperature nodes per configuration and numerical cancellation in statistical averages.
AI.method: Reformulates the Feynman path integral as Gaussian sampling of the neighborhood of each position configuration. Variance is derived from ring polymer statistics on a lattice, and the mean is obtained from the high temperature expansion of the Wigner-Kirkwood commutation function.
AI.result: Analytic and simulation results for the second virial coefficient of helium are compared to laboratory measurements, showing agreement.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Gaussian sampling approach offers a viable alternative to conventional path integral quantum Monte Carlo by circumventing key computational difficulties while maintaining accuracy against experimental data.

title: Atomically precise triple-step staircase on a vicinal silicon surface: Is it Si(5 5 7), Si(7 7 10) or Si(8 8 11)?
summary: Scanning tunneling microscopy studies of periodic arrays of triple steps fabricated on single-crystalline Si(5 5 7) wafers demonstrate several possible atomic structures of consecutive steps and Si(1 1 1) terraces maintaining the same periodicity on micrometer-sized surface areas. Detailed analysis of the atomically resolved data reveals the formation of Si(8 8 11) triple-step staircase with a period of 18b=5.99 nm in projection onto the terrace plane, where b=0.333 nm is the distance between atomic rows for the Si(1 1 1)1x1 surface. Schematic models for several possible configurations of either 7x7 or 5x5-reconstructed terraces and triple steps are proposed.

AI.tldr: STM studies of Si(5 5 7) wafers reveal triple-step staircases with Si(8 8 11) structure and 5.99 nm periodicity, along with proposed models for 7x7 or 5x5-reconstructed terraces and triple steps.
AI.motivation: To investigate atomic structures of periodic triple steps on Si(5 5 7) surfaces and understand possible configurations of consecutive steps and reconstructed terraces at the atomic scale.
AI.method: Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) with atomic resolution was used to study periodic triple steps on single-crystalline Si(5 5 7) wafers, revealing a Si(8 8 11) triple-step staircase with a projected period of 18b=5.99 nm.
AI.result: The atomic structure forms a Si(8 8 11) triple-step staircase with 18b=5.99 nm periodicity. Multiple possible configurations exist, involving either 7x7 or 5x5-reconstructed terraces combined with triple steps.
AI.conclusion: Periodic triple steps on Si(5 5 7) exhibit well-defined atomic structures with 5.99 nm periodicity, and schematic models for reconstructed terraces and triple steps are proposed.

title: Nanowire networks' interconnection graphs from their photomicrographs
summary: Self-assemblies of tunable units are being intensively studied as physical systems with signal-processing capabilities. Specifically, silver nanowire networks (AgNWNs) have demonstrated accumulation, non-linearity, and memory retention with multiple timescales, features that enable a wide variety of neuromorphic implementations. In this study, we aim to extract the interconnection scheme to analyze the experimentally obtained network architecture and, eventually, use it as input to a previously developed simulation platform. By post-processing photomicrographs of AgNWN, we present a pipeline optimized to extract the interconnection diagram, recognizing the intersections formed among the nanowires, to determine the associated graph for each physical sample. A graph is a collection of nodes and edges whose properties can be associated with different electrical responses. It is thus possible to study graphs' metrics, such as the degree distribution, community size, clustering coefficient, and path-length, to compare the experimental assemblies' attributes to those of topological models of reference. Small-world, modular, and scale-free are well-known structures in the field of mathematical graphs. By analyzing the degree distribution, the adjacency matrices, among other useful representation means, the experimental assemblies reveal similarities to both small-world and modular topologies. All the mentioned analyses were conducted considering the interconnection scheme obtained from zenithal-view optical images, which overestimates the number of NWs' interconnections (due to the impossibility of distinguishing real junctions from spurious cross-points between vertically displaced NWs). For that reason, this communication also studies the impact of artificially removing junctions from the resulting graphs on the previously calculated clustering coefficient and path length.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an image processing pipeline to extract the interconnection graph from silver nanowire networks (AgNWNs) from photomicrographs, analyzes network topology metrics (degree distribution, clustering coefficient, path length, community size), compares experimental networks to small-world, modular, and scale-free models, and examines the impact of overestimated junctions (due to vertical displacement ambiguity) on graph metrics by artificially removing spurious cross-points.
AI.motivation: To extract the interconnection scheme from experimentally obtained silver nanowire network architectures to enable analysis of their graph properties and provide realistic input for simulation platforms, addressing the challenge of distinguishing real electrical junctions from spurious cross-points in optical images.
AI.method: An image processing pipeline using post-processing of zenithal-view photomicrographs of AgNWNs to extract interconnection diagrams, recognize nanowire intersections, construct corresponding graphs, compute network metrics (degree distribution, clustering coefficient, path length, community size, adjacency matrices), compare to reference topological models (small-world, modular, scale-free), and artificially remove overestimated junctions to study metric sensitivity.
AI.result: Experimental AgNWN assemblies exhibit similarities to both small-world and modular topologies. The zenithal imaging overestimates interconnections due to inability to distinguish real junctions from vertically displaced cross-points. The study quantifies the impact of junction removal on clustering coefficient and path length metrics.
AI.conclusion: The extracted graph representation enables quantitative topological analysis of physical AgNWN assemblies, revealing small-world and modular characteristics, while highlighting the need to account for imaging-induced overestimation of junctions when interpreting network properties for neuromorphic applications.

title: Thermal and viscous contrast in quantum Hall scanning-probe images
comment: Comments: 18 pages, 5 figures; includes Supplemental Material
summary: Quantum Hall scanning images are often read as maps of a local potential, temperature, or viscosity, whereas a probe records a finite-resolution functional of a transport operator. We formulate this functional using Landau-level projection, a particle-number Ward identity, magnetization-subtracted thermoelectric transport, a hydrodynamic Stokes-Ohm inversion, and finite-tip Fisher information. Two results follow in complementary transport regimes. In the strong-field, sharp-Landau-level regime, the defect-induced thermoelectric and electrical Hall contrasts of a smooth scalar defect obey $δα_{xy}^{tr}/δσ_{xy}=(E_c-μ)/(eT)$. At the retained long-wavelength order, the orbital form factor, defect geometry, and common tip kernel cancel after the heat-magnetization current is removed, so the zero of the thermoelectric contrast is pinned by energy weighting at $E_c=μ$ rather than by defect shape. In the hydrodynamic regime, the measurable $q^2$ tensor amplitudes mix Hall, longitudinal, transverse, boundary, electrothermal, and kinetic channels, so a Hall-odd image is not by itself a Hall-viscosity measurement. For a representative graphene geometry, a Schur-complement fit against the stated nuisance library yields a conditional one-standard-deviation sensitivity of approximately 68 square nanometers at SNR0 = 200, with boundary slip the limiting nuisance. The framework turns visual interpretation of quantum Hall nanoscopy into a quantitative observability test for electrical, thermoelectric, and viscous response channels.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework for interpreting quantum Hall scanning images by formulating the probe response via Landau-level projection, Ward identities, magnetization-subtracted transport, Stokes-Ohm inversion, and Fisher information. It yields a pinned thermoelectric contrast ratio in the sharp-Landau-level regime and a Schur-complement sensitivity analysis in the hydrodynamic regime, demonstrating that Hall-odd images alone cannot uniquely measure Hall viscosity.
AI.motivation: Quantum Hall scanning images are often misinterpreted as direct maps of local potential, temperature, or viscosity, whereas the probe actually records a finite-resolution functional of a transport operator. A rigorous formulation is needed to properly interpret these images and extract quantitative transport information.
AI.method: The authors formulate the probe functional using Landau-level projection, a particle-number Ward identity, magnetization-subtracted thermoelectric transport, hydrodynamic Stokes-Ohm inversion, and finite-tip Fisher information. They analyze two complementary regimes: the strong-field sharp-Landau-level regime and the hydrodynamic regime.
AI.result: In the sharp-Landau-level regime, the defect-induced thermoelectric and electrical Hall contrasts satisfy δα_{xy}^{tr}/δσ_{xy} = (E_c-μ)/(eT), with the zero pinned at E_c=μ regardless of defect shape. In the hydrodynamic regime, the q^2 tensor amplitudes mix multiple channels, so Hall-odd images are not by themselves Hall-viscosity measurements. For a graphene geometry, a Schur-complement fit yields ~68 nm² conditional sensitivity at SNR0=200.
AI.conclusion: The framework turns visual interpretation of quantum Hall nanoscopy into a quantitative observability test for electrical, thermoelectric, and viscous response channels, enabling rigorous extraction of transport coefficients from imaging data.

title: Modeling rare-earth and energy materials supply chains under theoretical China-outer-Mongolia political reunification scenarios
summary: Critical rare earth elements, lithium, copper, and coal underpin global clean energy transitions and advanced manufacturing, yet China faces persistent supply volatility and resource security risks amid fragmented cross-border mineral trade with Outer Mongolia. This paper constructs a dynamic partial equilibrium Stackelberg supply chain model spanning 2026-2036, integrating three geographic nodes: Outer Mongolia's mineral extraction sector, Baotou's rare earth processing hub in Inner Mongolia, and residual demand from the Rest of the World (RoW). The model endogenizes core mechanisms including mineral supply curves constrained by infrastructure stock, lagged capital accumulation, Leontief processing production functions, profit-driven investment, and optimal export tax policy maximizing China's discounted social welfare. Three comparative scenarios are calibrated and simulated: a baseline status-quo trade framework, deep Sino-Mongolian resource integration, and a delayed cross-border infrastructure counterfactual.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a dynamic Stackelberg supply chain model (2026-2036) analyzing China's critical mineral trade with Outer Mongolia, examining three scenarios: baseline trade, deep integration, and delayed infrastructure.
AI.motivation: China faces supply volatility and resource security risks in critical minerals (rare earths, lithium, copper, coal) due to fragmented cross-border trade with Outer Mongolia, despite these resources being essential for clean energy transitions and advanced manufacturing.
AI.method: A dynamic partial equilibrium Stackelberg supply chain model spanning 2026-2036 with three geographic nodes (Outer Mongolia extraction, Baotou processing, Rest of World demand), incorporating mineral supply curves constrained by infrastructure, lagged capital accumulation, Leontief production functions, profit-driven investment, and optimal export tax policy maximizing China's discounted social welfare.
AI.result: Three calibrated scenarios (baseline, deep integration, delayed infrastructure counterfactual) simulated to quantify outcomes under different trade and policy frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a framework for assessing optimal trade policies and infrastructure investments to enhance China's resource security in critical minerals.

title: Stochastic Resetting: A Non-Equilibrium Framework for Prediction, Inference and Design
summary: Stochastic resetting has evolved from a simple model of diffusive search acceleration into a general framework for predicting, inferring, and controlling stochastic dynamics far from equilibrium. Its defining features, i.e., the creation of non-equilibrium steady states and the acceleration of first-passage kinetics, are increasingly relevant across physical chemistry, from biological restart mechanisms to molecular simulations and colloidal experiments. We review the renewal theory underlying stochastic resetting and show how it enables prediction of reset dynamics from properties of the underlying process, while also allowing the latter to be inferred from the resetting-accelerated dynamics. We then discuss applications to state preparation, enhanced sampling, kinetic inference, and training and sampling of machine learning models. Finally, we review recent advances in adaptive resetting, environmental feedback, many-body dynamics, and thermodynamic costs of resetting. These developments establish new opportunities for controlling stochastic dynamics with resetting across theory, simulations, and experiments.

AI.tldr: This review covers stochastic resetting as a framework for understanding and controlling non-equilibrium stochastic dynamics, including renewal theory, applications in state preparation, enhanced sampling, kinetic inference, machine learning, and recent advances in adaptive resetting, feedback, many-body systems, and thermodynamics.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive review of stochastic resetting, which has evolved from a simple search-acceleration model into a general framework for predicting, inferring, and controlling stochastic dynamics far from equilibrium, with growing relevance across physical chemistry.
AI.method: The review systematically examines renewal theory underlying stochastic resetting, showing how it enables prediction of reset dynamics from process properties and inference of underlying processes from resetting-accelerated dynamics. It covers applications in state preparation, enhanced sampling, kinetic inference, and machine learning, as well as recent advances in adaptive resetting, environmental feedback, many-body dynamics, and thermodynamic costs.
AI.result: Stochastic resetting creates non-equilibrium steady states and accelerates first-passage kinetics. The renewal framework allows both forward prediction and inverse inference. Key applications include controlled state preparation, enhanced sampling efficiency, kinetic parameter inference, and improved training/sampling of ML models. Recent advances address adaptive strategies, feedback mechanisms, collective behaviors, and thermodynamic cost analysis.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic resetting establishes new opportunities for controlling stochastic dynamics across theory, simulations, and experiments, with broad applicability from molecular to colloidal systems.

title: Simulating neural network criticality and resource dynamics with Rydberg gases
summary: Efficient operation of neural networks has been linked to criticality in their underlying non-equilibrium excitation dynamics. However, obtaining experimental evidence of this conjecture remains challenging due to limited control and undersampling in biological systems. Here, we experimentally explore neural network criticality using an ultracold Rydberg gas as a highly controllable simulator. We highlight the similarity of the excitation spreading via Rydberg facilitation and the synaptic connection of spiking activity of neurons, giving rise to distinct absorbing and active phases. We systematically explore and resolve criticality criteria, including power-law scaling of excitation avalanches and the emergence of universal avalanche shape collapse. Crucially, we implement a controlled gain mechanism to compensate for atom loss, mimicking metabolic resource replenishment and stabilizing the system in a controlled non-equilibrium steady state. We find peak temporal correlations at the critical point and stochastic oscillations with dragon king avalanches in the active phase, consistent with predictions for systems orbiting criticality. Our work establishes facilitated Rydberg gases as a platform for investigating criticality, resource dynamics, and emergent oscillations in neural networks.

AI.tldr: Using an ultracold Rydberg gas as a controllable simulator, this paper experimentally demonstrates neural network criticality, showing power-law scaling of excitation avalanches, universal avalanche shape collapse, peak temporal correlations at the critical point, and dragon king avalanches in the active phase, with a controlled gain mechanism mimicking metabolic resource replenishment.
AI.motivation: Efficient neural network operation is theoretically linked to criticality in non-equilibrium excitation dynamics, but obtaining experimental evidence remains challenging due to limited control and undersampling in biological systems. The authors address this gap by developing a highly controllable artificial system.
AI.method: The authors use an ultracold Rydberg gas as a simulator where Rydberg facilitation mimics synaptic connection of spiking neurons. They systematically explore criticality criteria (power-law scaling, avalanche shape collapse), implement a controlled gain mechanism to compensate for atom loss (mimicking metabolic resource replenishment), and stabilize the system in a controlled non-equilibrium steady state.
AI.result: They observe power-law scaling of excitation avalanches, universal avalanche shape collapse, peak temporal correlations at the critical point, and stochastic oscillations with dragon king avalanches in the active phase, consistent with predictions for systems orbiting criticality.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes facilitated Rydberg gases as a platform for investigating criticality, resource dynamics, and emergent oscillations in neural networks, providing experimental evidence for the criticality hypothesis that was previously difficult to obtain in biological systems.

title: Delayed Coupling Restores Ising Phase Dynamics in Physical Oscillator Networks
summary: Oscillator-based Ising machines, in which the phases of coupled self-sustaining oscillators evolve toward decreasing an Ising Hamiltonian, are commonly interpreted as physical realizations of the Ising model. This interpretation, however, requires the phase dynamics generated by the physical oscillator network to match a prescribed Ising dynamics. Here we show that this correspondence is generally not guaranteed. For arbitrary self-sustaining oscillators under weak coupling, we derive the physical phase interaction from the harmonic overlap between the injected waveform and the perturbation projection vector (also referred to as impulse sensitivity function). We find that uncompensated harmonic phase mismatches between these two quantities generate even components in the physical coupling function, causing a network with the correct coupling topology to implement a non-Ising dynamics. We further show that delayed coupling provides a universal phase-compensation mechanism. For a fixed delay, we derive a condition on the delay under which the even components is minimized in the sense of L2-norm, and oscillator examples confirm that the predicted delay substantially suppresses the even components and brings the realized coupling function closer to the prescribed odd interaction. We then show that a periodically modulated delay can, under suitable moment conditions, eliminate the even components in the phase dynamics. These results establish a general design principle for implementing prescribed energy-based dynamics in physical oscillator networks.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that oscillator-based Ising machines do not inherently implement true Ising dynamics due to harmonic phase mismatches, and proposes delayed coupling as a universal compensation mechanism to suppress non-Ising (even) components, culminating in a design principle for realizing prescribed energy-based dynamics in physical oscillator networks.
AI.motivation: Oscillator-based Ising machines are commonly assumed to physically realize the Ising model, but this correspondence is not guaranteed. The authors aim to identify the conditions under which physical oscillator networks actually implement Ising dynamics and to develop a general design principle for correcting deviations.
AI.method: The authors derive the physical phase interaction from the harmonic overlap between the injected waveform and the perturbation projection vector (impulse sensitivity function). They analyze the effect of uncompensated harmonic phase mismatches, which generate even components in the coupling function leading to non-Ising dynamics. They propose delayed coupling as a universal compensation mechanism and derive a delay condition that minimizes even components in the L2-norm sense, as well as a periodically modulated delay scheme that can eliminate even components under appropriate moment conditions.
AI.result: Uncompensated harmonic phase mismatches between the injected waveform and the perturbation projection vector produce even components in the physical coupling function, causing non-Ising dynamics despite correct coupling topology. A fixed optimal delay minimizes these even components (L2-norm), and a periodically modulated delay can eliminate them entirely under suitable moment conditions. Oscillator examples confirm the predicted delay substantially suppresses even components.
AI.conclusion: These findings establish a general design principle for implementing prescribed energy-based dynamics in physical oscillator networks, specifically showing how delayed coupling can correct the non-Ising behavior inherent in weakly coupled oscillator networks.

title: A Disconnected Superconducting Regime at the Parent Limit of Infinite-Layer Nickelates
summary: Infinite-layer nickelates have been widely viewed as cuprate analogs in which superconductivity emerges and forms a superconducting dome centered around 10-20% cation substitution. Here we show that pristine and stoichiometric PrNiO2, without cation substitution, exhibits intrinsic superconductivity characterized by zero resistance and diamagnetism in uncapped films. Through heterostructure engineering, we further exclude an interfacial origin of the superconductivity. Remarkably, zero-resistance superconductivity is consistently observed in trivalent-substituted PrNiO2, whereas it is rapidly suppressed by dilute divalent substitution. Combined with angle-resolved photoemission studies, these results indicate that such a new superconducting regime is confined to within 3% additional hole doping from pristine PrNiO2. Furthermore, this phase is separated from the previously established superconducting dome around ~ 20% divalent doping by a non-superconducting region in the phase diagram, and is further distinguished by a remarkably stronger upper-critical-field anisotropy. These findings establish a unique separated superconducting regime, suggesting that infinite-layer nickelates are not merely cuprate analogs but host distinct superconducting physics.

AI.tldr: Pristine PrNiO2 exhibits intrinsic superconductivity without cation substitution, forming a distinct superconducting regime separate from the known dome, with strong upper-critical-field anisotropy, indicating nickelates are not mere cuprate analogs.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether pristine, stoichiometric PrNiO2 (without cation substitution) can exhibit intrinsic superconductivity, and to characterize the nature of this superconductivity in comparison to the established doped superconducting dome in infinite-layer nickelates.
AI.method: Heterostructure engineering to exclude interfacial effects; transport measurements (zero resistance, diamagnetism) on uncapped films; angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES); systematic substitution with trivalent and divalent cations to map phase diagram.
AI.result: Pristine PrNiO2 shows zero-resistance and diamagnetic superconductivity. Superconductivity persists under trivalent substitution but is rapidly suppressed by dilute divalent doping. The superconducting regime is confined to within 3% additional hole doping from pristine PrNiO2, and is separated from the conventional ~20% divalent doping dome by a non-superconducting region, exhibiting stronger upper-critical-field anisotropy.
AI.conclusion: Infinite-layer nickelates host a distinct, separated superconducting regime that is not simply cuprate-like, suggesting unique superconducting physics beyond the cuprate analog framework.

title: $J_{1} - J_{2} - δ$ model on a square lattice: From Altermagnet to Columnar antiferromagnet via quantum disordered phase
summary: Altermagnetism in the case of local-moment magnets is characterized by zero net magnetization and splitting of opposite chirality magnon bands in the absence of any spin-anisotropic interactions or external field. In this work we investigate the robustness of altermagnets against quantum fluctuations arising from magnetic frustration. We consider a Heisenberg model on a square lattice with two different types of second-neighbor interactions, as in a checkboard pattern, in addition to the nearest-neighbor interaction. This model continuously interpolates between the $J_{1}-J_{2}$ Heisenberg model on the square lattice and the Heisenberg model on the checkerboard lattice. For weaker second-neighbor interactions a Néel-type altermagnet phase is realized. On the other hand, for stronger second-neighbor interactions a columnar antiferromagnet emerges. Using linear spin-wave theory we calculate the magnon dispersion, order parameter, static and dynamical structure factors for the two magnetic phases. Further, we show that there is an intermediate quantum disordered phase separating the two magnetic phases, which is connected to the one realized in the $J_{1}-J_{2}$ model. The quantum disordered region is further stabilized as we tune towards the checkerboard lattice limit.

AI.tldr: This paper explores altermagnetism in frustrated Heisenberg models on a square lattice with checkerboard-like second-neighbor interactions, showing that altermagnetic order persists at weaker second-neighbor couplings but gives way to columnar antiferromagnetism and a quantum disordered phase at stronger frustration, especially near the checkerboard lattice limit.
AI.motivation: To investigate the robustness of altermagnets against quantum fluctuations induced by magnetic frustration, particularly in systems with competing interactions on a square lattice with checkerboard-like second-neighbor couplings.
AI.method: Linear spin-wave theory is applied to a Heisenberg model on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor and two types of second-neighbor interactions (checkerboard pattern), interpolating between the J1-J2 square lattice and the checkerboard lattice models. Magnon dispersion, order parameter, static and dynamical structure factors are calculated.
AI.result: A Néel-type altermagnet phase exists for weaker second-neighbor interactions, while a columnar antiferromagnet emerges for stronger interactions. An intermediate quantum disordered phase separates these two magnetic phases, which is connected to that of the J1-J2 model and is further stabilized toward the checkerboard lattice limit.
AI.conclusion: Altermagnetism can survive under moderate frustration, but strong frustration destabilizes it, leading to a quantum disordered regime. The checkerboard lattice limit enhances the quantum disordered region.

title: Representation-Dependent Machine Learning of the Isotropic-Nematic Transition in the Lebwohl-Lasher Model
summary: Machine-learning detection of phase transitions depends not only on the learning algorithm, but also on whether the input representation preserves the symmetries of the system. We examine this for the weak first-order isotropic--nematic transition of the three-dimensional Lebwohl--Lasher model, whose apolar and continuously degenerate nematic phase makes raw molecular configurations a challenging input for unsupervised learning. Principal component analysis (PCA) and a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) fail to identify the transition from raw configurations because rotationally equivalent nematic states can appear far apart in the input space. When the same configurations are transformed into a rotationally invariant local-correlation representation, both methods recover transition-sensitive signatures and bimodal coexistence distributions. A supervised three-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN), by contrast, accurately predicts the scalar order parameter from raw configurations when given order-parameter labels. The Lebwohl-Lasher model therefore separates unsupervised phase discovery from supervised order-parameter regression and shows that symmetry-respecting input representations are needed for unsupervised machine learning in orientationally ordered systems.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised learning (PCA, CAE) fails to detect the isotropic–nematic transition of the Lebwohl–Lasher model from raw molecular configurations due to rotational symmetry, but succeeds when using rotationally invariant local-correlation features; supervised CNNs can predict the order parameter from raw data if given labels.
AI.motivation: To understand how input representation and symmetry preservation affect machine-learning detection of phase transitions, especially for orientationally ordered systems with continuous rotational degeneracy.
AI.method: Applied PCA, convolutional autoencoder (CAE), and supervised 3D CNN to raw and rotationally invariant local-correlation representations of the Lebwohl–Lasher model's configurations.
AI.result: Unsupervised methods (PCA, CAE) fail on raw configurations but succeed on rotationally invariant representations; supervised CNN succeeds on raw data when given order-parameter labels.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-respecting input representations are required for unsupervised phase discovery in orientationally ordered systems, while supervised methods can bypass this requirement with labeled data.

title: Valley polarization, Rashba interaction, and weak altermagnetism in inversion-asymmetric MnPS$_\text{3}|$WS$_\text{2}$ van der Waals heterostructures
summary: The deliberate breaking of inversion ($\mathcal{P}$) symmetry in antiferromagnets has recently emerged as an effective means to induce various features, such as the emergence of Berry curvature, spin-valley locking, magnetoelectric coupling, and the transition from conventional antiferromagnetism to altermagnetism. Conversely, in non-magnetic systems, inversion symmetry breaking in the presence of strong spin-orbit interaction (SOI) gives rise to momentum-dependent spin splitting via the Rashba effect, enabling tunable spin polarization through external electric fields. Motivated by recent advances in two-dimensional materials, we perform first-principles calculations based on density functional theory to investigate the van der Waals (vdW) heterostructure formed by a $\mathcal{P}$-symmetric MnPS$_3$ monolayer and a WS$_2$ monolayer. We demonstrate that the interface hosts a rich interplay of emergent phenomena, including an altermagnetic phase, Rashba spin splitting, spin-valley locking, and valley polarization. Our results demonstrate that the heterostructure exhibits semiconducting behavior with a direct band gap of approximately 1.65~eV and a type-I band alignment. Remarkably, the electronic structure and band alignment can be effectively tuned between type-I and type-II regimes via an external electric field and in-plane biaxial strain. Furthermore, field-induced modulation enables strong control over the altermagnetic phase and the valley splitting. These findings establish the proposed vdW heterostructure as a highly tunable platform with significant potential for spintronic and valleytronic applications.

AI.tldr: First-principles study of a MnPS₃/WS₂ van der Waals heterostructure reveals that interface-induced inversion symmetry breaking leads to an altermagnetic phase, Rashba spin splitting, spin-valley locking, and valley polarization, with electronic structure and band alignment tunable via electric field and biaxial strain, promising for spintronics and valleytronics.
AI.motivation: To explore whether deliberately breaking inversion symmetry in antiferromagnets via van der Waals heterostructures can induce emergent phenomena (altermagnetism, Rashba effect, spin-valley locking, and valley polarization) for spintronic and valleytronic applications.
AI.method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) on a van der Waals heterostructure composed of a 𝒫-symmetric MnPS₃ monolayer and a WS₂ monolayer.
AI.result: The heterostructure exhibits semiconducting behavior with a direct band gap of ~1.65 eV and type-I band alignment. The electronic structure and band alignment are tunable between type-I and type-II regimes via external electric field and in-plane biaxial strain. Field-induced modulation also enables strong control over the altermagnetic phase and valley splitting.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MnPS₃/WS₂ vdW heterostructure is a highly tunable platform with significant potential for spintronic and valleytronic applications.

title: Point Group Equivariant Graph Neural Networks for Materials
summary: Equivariant graph neural networks have proven effective tools for inference of material's properties directly from their structure. Traditionally, these have been applied such that they respect full $O(3)$ equivariance, so that any rotation or reflection of the input structure is respected in the model's output. While this works for general arrangements of atoms, additional symmetries of atomistic systems are left unleveraged. Furthermore, any symmetries of the filter functions are implicitly learned from the full dataset and not strictly enforced. In this work, we introduce point-group symmetry aware equivariant graph neural networks (PGEqNN) for materials science, with filter functions aligned with symmetry-aware indices for greater granularity in predictive tasks. With this architecture, we show that most of the predictive power of equivariant networks for tensorial elastic and dielectric datasets lies in the trivial subspaces of the point-group adapted bases. Exploiting this, an $A_1$-restricted variant matches or improves on its full point-group and $SO(3)$-partitioned counterparts while training fewer active parameters, yielding leaner models of equal accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PGEqNN, a point-group symmetry aware equivariant graph neural network for materials science that aligns filter functions with symmetry-aware indices. It shows that most predictive power for tensorial properties lies in trivial subspaces, and an A1-restricted variant achieves equal or better accuracy with fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Traditional O(3)-equivariant GNNs for materials property prediction leave additional symmetries of atomistic systems unleveraged and do not strictly enforce symmetries of filter functions, instead learning them implicitly from data.
AI.method: PGEqNN uses point-group symmetry aware filter functions aligned with symmetry-adapted bases, enabling finer granularity in predictive tasks. An A1-restricted variant focuses on trivial subspaces of the point-group adapted bases.
AI.result: The predictive power of equivariant networks for tensorial elastic and dielectric datasets primarily resides in the trivial subspaces. The A1-restricted variant matches or improves accuracy while training fewer active parameters.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging point-group symmetry yields leaner models with equal or better accuracy compared to full O(3)/SO(3)-equivariant counterparts.

title: Observation of Critical Current Minimum in Super-Honeycomb Josephson Junction Arrays
summary: Superconductor-semiconductor Josephson junction arrays are a uniquely tunable platform for studying collective quantum phenomena, particularly in the regime where localized Andreev bound states can hybridize across the lattice when the physical separation between adjacent junctions is smaller than their coherence length ($ξ_{\text{ABS}}>d_{\text{JJ}}$). Here, we investigate three distinct Al-InAs Josephson junction arrays: a square array and super-honeycomb array fabricated within this ${ξ_{\text{ABS}}>d_{\text{JJ}}}$ regime, as well as a larger-spacing super-honeycomb control device designed such that $ξ_{\text{ABS}}\lesssim\!~d_{\text{JJ}}$. Under an out-of-plane field, critical current peaks emerge at rational filling factors, reflecting stable vortex configurations in the lattices. In the super-honeycomb lattice, vortices localize to distinct non-identical plaquettes at different filling factors, as predicted by frustrated XY model simulations. A rotating in-plane field yields periodic critical current oscillations that reflect the Rashba spin-orbit coupling inherent to the InAs quantum well. Surprisingly, at $f = 1$, the closely spaced super-honeycomb array exhibits a distinct critical current minimum as the magnitude of the in-plane field increases, a signature absent in the square array and large-spacing super-honeycomb array. These results indicate that this signature is jointly influenced by the unique geometry of the super-honeycomb vortex lattice and by long-range inter-junction hybridization.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Al-InAs Josephson junction arrays in the regime where Andreev bound states hybridize across adjacent junctions (ξ_ABS > d_JJ). Square and super-honeycomb arrays show critical current peaks at rational filling factors under out-of-plane fields, with vortices localizing to distinct plaquettes in the super-honeycomb lattice. In-plane field oscillations reveal Rashba spin-orbit coupling, and at filling factor f=1, the closely spaced super-honeycomb array uniquely exhibits a critical current minimum, attributed to geometry and inter-junction hybridization.
AI.motivation: To explore collective quantum phenomena in superconductor-semiconductor Josephson junction arrays where localized Andreev bound states can hybridize across the lattice when the physical separation between adjacent junctions is smaller than their coherence length (ξ_ABS > d_JJ).
AI.method: Fabrication and measurement of three distinct Al-InAs Josephson junction arrays (square, super-honeycomb in the ξ_ABS > d_JJ regime, and a larger-spacing super-honeycomb control device with ξ_ABS ≲ d_JJ). Out-of-plane field was applied to observe critical current peaks at rational filling factors, and rotating in-plane field was used to probe periodic critical current oscillations. Frustrated XY model simulations were used for comparison.
AI.result: Critical current peaks emerged at rational filling factors reflecting stable vortex configurations. In the super-honeycomb lattice, vortices localized to distinct non-identical plaquettes at different filling factors. Rotating in-plane field yielded periodic critical current oscillations reflecting Rashba spin-orbit coupling. At f=1, the closely spaced super-honeycomb array uniquely showed a distinct critical current minimum as in-plane field magnitude increased, absent in the square and large-spacing super-honeycomb arrays.
AI.conclusion: The unique critical current minimum signature at f=1 in the closely spaced super-honeycomb array is jointly influenced by the super-honeycomb vortex lattice geometry and long-range inter-junction hybridization (ξ_ABS > d_JJ regime).

title: anyakrakusuma: A Python Library for Entropic Schrödinger Bridges on Idealized Geometries
summary: We present anyakrakusuma, an open-source Python library that solves the discrete static Schrödinger bridge problem, the entropically regularized counterpart of optimal transport, through a log-domain Sinkhorn--Knopp iteration and reconstructs the entropic interpolation between two empirical point clouds. The solver is paired with a diagnostic pipeline that characterizes the optimal coupling and the intermediate distributions through information-theoretic and geometric measures. We exercise the library on four idealized planar cases spanning a circle-to-circle dilation, a spiral-to-mixture fragmentation, a rigid reorientation of two moons, and a Lissajous-to-trefoil deformation. The log-domain formulation is necessary rather than merely convenient at the parameters studied, where the cost-to-regularization ratio reaches four hundred and the Gibbs kernel underflows double precision across most of its range; the iteration nonetheless attains a marginal residual of $10^{-9}$ and unit marginal fidelity in every case. Residual histories decay geometrically over approximately eight decades at per-iteration contraction factors between $0.966$ and $0.976$, which are local rates near the fixed point that lie many orders of magnitude below the worst-case Hilbert-metric bound. The covariance analysis recovers an imposed ninety-degree reorientation to within $0.07^\circ$, roughly forty times smaller than its uncertainty, across a masked interval of near-isotropy on which the principal axis is unobservable. The diagnostics are reported with explicit attention to the regimes in which each is well defined, including the differential entropy, which is meaningful only on the open interpolation interval. The presented cases are constructed rather than measured; quantitative application to empirical point clouds requires further study.

AI.tldr: anyakrakusuma is an open-source Python library for solving the discrete static Schrödinger bridge problem via log-domain Sinkhorn–Knopp iteration. It reconstructs entropic interpolation between empirical point clouds, includes information-theoretic and geometric diagnostics, and demonstrates robust convergence on four planar test cases with extreme cost-to-regularization ratios up to 400, achieving high marginal fidelity and sub-degree angular accuracy.
AI.motivation: To provide a numerically stable, open-source implementation for the entropically regularized optimal transport (Schrödinger bridge) problem, especially under regimes where the Gibbs kernel underflows double precision, and to pair the solver with a rigorous diagnostic framework for characterizing optimal couplings and intermediate distributions.
AI.method: The library uses a log-domain Sinkhorn–Knopp iteration to solve the discrete static Schrödinger bridge problem, avoiding numerical underflow. It includes a diagnostic pipeline with information-theoretic and geometric measures. Four planar test cases (circle-to-circle dilation, spiral-to-mixture fragmentation, rigid reorientation of two moons, Lissajous-to-trefoil deformation) are used to evaluate performance.
AI.result: The log-domain iteration converges at cost-to-regularization ratios up to 400 where standard Gibbs kernel underflows. It achieves marginal residual of 10^{-9} and unit marginal fidelity. Residual contraction factors are 0.966–0.976, far below the worst-case Hilbert-metric bound. Covariance analysis recovers a 90° rotation to within 0.07°, ~40× below uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The log-domain Sinkhorn–Knopp formulation is necessary and effective for high-cost-to-regularization regimes. The diagnostic pipeline provides meaningful measures when applied in appropriate regimes (e.g., differential entropy only on the open interpolation interval). The method is demonstrated on constructed cases; quantitative application to empirical data requires further study.

title: SONIC: Symmetry-Oriented Non-redundant Internal Coordinates
comment: 64 pages, 6 figures; Supporting Information supplied as a 7-page ancillary PDF; code and reproducibility materials are described in the manuscript
summary: Internal coordinates are the natural language of molecular structure, but automatic non-redundant constructions remain difficult for fused rings, high coordination, molecular symmetry, and weakly bound fragments. We present SONIC (Symmetry-Oriented Non-redundant Internal Coordinates), implemented in SMITH, as a deterministic construction of localized, symmetry-adapted generalized internal coordinates. SMITH accepts a frozen molecular state, supplied topology or primitives, or Cartesian input through a revision-pinned standalone perception kernel. It classifies ordinary primitives, adds chemically typed special and composite families, protects ring and fragment coordinates, and performs block-local rank reduction using analytic Wilson B rows. Local pseudosymmetry orders center, ring, and bond domains, while exact molecular point-group projection is applied within homogeneous blocks. The output is a frozen coordinate contract with human-readable decompositions, symmetry and rank diagnostics, analytic first derivatives, and optional Gaussian 16 serialization. Optimization, internal-to-Cartesian realization, force fields, and higher-order Hessian transformations remain downstream responsibilities. Validation covers acyclic, fused, bridged, high-coordinate, non-covalent, and eta3 metal-complex cases, including rotation/permutation invariance, Python/Fortran checks, and independent GIC evaluation.

AI.tldr: SONIC (Symmetry-Oriented Non-redundant Internal Coordinates), implemented in SMITH, deterministically constructs localized, symmetry-adapted generalized internal coordinates for molecular systems, handling fused rings, high coordination, symmetry, and weakly bound fragments via block-local rank reduction and point-group projection.
AI.motivation: Internal coordinates are natural for molecular structure description, but automatic non-redundant construction remains challenging for fused rings, high coordination, molecular symmetry, and weakly bound fragments.
AI.method: SMITH classifies ordinary primitives, adds chemically typed special and composite families, protects ring and fragment coordinates, performs block-local rank reduction using analytic Wilson B rows, applies local pseudosymmetry ordering and exact molecular point-group projection within homogeneous blocks.
AI.result: Outputs a frozen coordinate contract with human-readable decompositions, symmetry and rank diagnostics, analytic first derivatives, and optional Gaussian 16 serialization. Validated on acyclic, fused, bridged, high-coordinate, non-covalent, and eta3 metal-complex cases with rotation/permutation invariance and independent GIC evaluation.
AI.conclusion: SONIC/SMITH provides a robust deterministic framework for generating non-redundant symmetry-adapted internal coordinates; optimization, internal-to-Cartesian realization, force fields, and higher-order Hessian transformations remain downstream.

title: Order of Magnitude Improved Optical Trapping of Molecules Through Transverse Cooling
summary: We demonstrate a two-dimensional Sisyphus laser cooling method that increases the number of strontium monohydroxide (SrOH) molecules loaded into a magneto-optical trap by a factor of 12. Subsequent loading into an optical dipole trap (ODT) achieves $2.2 (3)\times10^4$ ultracold SrOH molecules with a peak density of $\sim2(1)\times10^{10}~\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$. The lifetime of molecules in the ODT is limited by two-body collisions characterized by a measured collision rate constant $β\sim 4\times10^{-10}~\mathrm{cm^3/s}$. The cooling method developed here is generally applicable to all known cases of direct molecular laser cooling, including symmetric and asymmetric top molecules. Increases in trapped molecule number will directly improve the search for ultralight dark matter, position polyatomic molecules as a platform for probing CP-violating new particles with masses $\gg$10 TeV, and facilitate a broad range of further research in quantum science.

AI.tldr: A 2D Sisyphus laser cooling method increases SrOH molecule loading into a MOT by 12×, yielding 2.2×10⁴ ultracold molecules in an optical dipole trap with peak density ~2×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ and two-body collision-limited lifetime (β~4×10⁻¹⁰ cm³/s).
AI.motivation: To increase the number of ultracold polyatomic molecules loaded into traps, enabling improved sensitivity for ultralight dark matter searches, CP-violating new particle probes, and quantum science research.
AI.method: Two-dimensional Sisyphus laser cooling technique applied to SrOH molecules, followed by loading into a magneto-optical trap and then an optical dipole trap.
AI.result: 12-fold increase in MOT loading; 2.2(3)×10⁴ ultracold SrOH molecules in ODT; peak density ~2(1)×10¹⁰ cm⁻³; two-body collision rate constant β~4×10⁻¹⁰ cm³/s.
AI.conclusion: The cooling method is generally applicable to all directly laser-coolable molecules (symmetric and asymmetric tops), and the increased yields directly benefit dark matter searches, CP-violation physics, and broader quantum science.

title: A Compact Reconfigurable Antenna for Single-RF-Chain Passive Multi-Target DOA Estimation
summary: This work proposes a compact and hardware-efficient frequency- and radiation-pattern-reconfigurable antenna (FPRA) for passive multi-target direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation using a single receive RF chain. The antenna consists of a sectorized circular patch loaded with 16 PIN diodes. By switching the diode states, the current-concentration boundary on the patch is shifted, enabling reconfiguration of both the operating frequency and radiation pattern. With a single receive RF chain, the proposed antenna achieves beam scanning from -40 degrees to 40 degrees and provides multiple operating frequencies across the S- and C-bands. Based on these reconfigurable observation states, radiation-pattern switching is used to emulate the spatial sampling of a conventional antenna array, while multi-frequency observations introduce phase diversity to reduce the correlation among echoes from multiple passive targets illuminated by the same transmitter. Experimental results demonstrate that the combined virtual spatial sampling and frequency diversity enable passive multi-target DOA estimation without a conventional antenna array or multiple receive RF chains. The proposed FPRA offers a compact and hardware-efficient sensing solution for future integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a compact, reconfigurable antenna (FPRA) with 16 PIN diodes that enables passive multi-target DOA estimation using only a single receive RF chain, combining pattern reconfiguration for virtual spatial sampling and frequency diversity for echo decorrelation.
AI.motivation: To enable passive multi-target DOA estimation in a compact and hardware-efficient manner without requiring a conventional antenna array or multiple receive RF chains, addressing the size, cost, and complexity constraints of future ISAC systems.
AI.method: A sectorized circular patch antenna loaded with 16 PIN diodes is designed. By switching diode states, the current-concentration boundary shifts to reconfigure both frequency and radiation pattern. Radiation-pattern switching emulates spatial sampling of an antenna array, while multi-frequency observations introduce phase diversity to decorrelate echoes from multiple passive targets.
AI.result: Beam scanning from -40° to 40° is achieved; multiple operating frequencies across S- and C-bands are provided; combined virtual spatial sampling and frequency diversity enable passive multi-target DOA estimation with a single receive RF chain.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FPRA offers a compact and hardware-efficient sensing solution for future ISAC systems, eliminating the need for conventional antenna arrays or multiple RF chains for multi-target DOA estimation.

title: Unconventional superconductivity in ScIr$_2$ chiral crystal with a kagome lattice
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures; accepted by Adv. Mater
summary: Materials with a kagome lattice host exotic quantum phenomena driven by the interplay between band topology, spin-orbit coupling, magnetism, and electronic correlations. While magnetism of kagome materials has been widely investigated, their unconventional superconductivity (SC) remains largely unexplored due to the limited availability of suitable materials. Here, we report evidence of unconventional SC in the ScIr$_{2-x}$Si$_{x}$ family by combining muon-spin spectroscopy measurements with band-structure calculations. The parent ScIr$_2$ undergoes a structural phase transition from a high-$T$ cubic- to a low-$T$ rhombohedral phase, while the Ir kagome layer remains, albeit slightly distorted. Although the structural transition is suppressed by Si substitution, the superconducting pairing of ScIr$_{2-x}$Si$_{x}$ remains well described by a two-gap model. Since at least one of the gaps has nodes, this indicates an unconventional SC. Its unconventional nature can be explained by the distinct flat bands occurring near the Fermi level, leading to strong electronic correlations in the ScIr$_{2-x}$Si$_{x}$ family. Moreover, the low-$T$ phase of ScIr$_2$ exhibits an Ir chiral chain; therefore, it can be classified as a topological chiral crystal. Overall, the unusual properties of the ScIr$_{2-x}$Si$_{x}$ family make it an interesting, albeit rare, system for studying the interplay between unconventional SC, flat bands, and chirality.

AI.tldr: The paper reports evidence of unconventional superconductivity in the ScIr₂₋ₓSiₓ kagome family, characterized by two-gap pairing with nodes, flat bands near the Fermi level, and chiral structural features, making it a rare platform to study the interplay between superconductivity, flat bands, and chirality.
AI.motivation: Unconventional superconductivity in kagome materials remains largely unexplored due to the scarcity of suitable materials, despite the widespread investigation of magnetism in such systems.
AI.method: The study combines muon-spin spectroscopy measurements with band-structure calculations to investigate the electronic and superconducting properties of ScIr₂₋ₓSiₓ.
AI.result: Si substitution suppresses the structural phase transition of parent ScIr₂, but the superconducting pairing remains two-gap with at least one nodal gap, indicating unconventional SC. Flat bands near the Fermi level drive strong electronic correlations.
AI.conclusion: ScIr₂₋ₓSiₓ is a rare system for studying the interplay between unconventional superconductivity, flat bands, and chirality, with the low-T phase of ScIr₂ classified as a topological chiral crystal.

title: Stroboscopic stability of a Floquet chiral spin liquid beyond the folding frequency
summary: We study the two-step Floquet dynamics of the chiral $J_1$-$J_2$-$K$ Heisenberg model on the $4\times4$ torus, alternating its non-chiral Heisenberg part $H_{\rm AF}$ and its chiral plaquette part $H_K$, at the parameter point where the static model (recovered in the infinite frequency limit) hosts a quasi-degenerate, spectrally isolated chiral-spin-liquid (CSL) topological doublet. The one-period propagator is computed exactly in all momentum/rotation symmetry sectors. It is shown that, decreasing the frequency, the topological doublet survives the drive far beyond the frequency $ω_{\mathrm{res}}\simeq 11.5 J_1$ at which folded states first cross it in quasienergy: the time-averaged energy of the Floquet eigenstates, which orders the folded Floquet spectrum, shows that the doublet remains the isolated bottom of the spectrum down to $ω\simeq6J_1$, while stroboscopic time evolution over thousands of periods shows no heating for $ω\gtrsim ω_{\mathrm{res}}$ and only slow absorption below. The quasienergy resonances that occur in the folded regime are invisible in the average energy, identifying them as parametrically weak avoided crossings. We argue that this mechanism -- stability controlled by local energy scales rather than by the extensive many-body bandwidth -- is precisely the one expected to survive in the thermodynamic limit, where a prethermal Floquet CSL should persist for $ω$ above a threshold set by local scales, with heating times exponentially long in $ω/J_1$. Consistently, the optimal $D=3$ chiral PEPS of the static problem still describes the driven doublet deep in the folded regime, with an essentially unchanged local tensor.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a two-step Floquet-driven chiral J1-J2-K Heisenberg model on a 4×4 torus, showing that the topological chiral-spin-liquid (CSL) doublet remains stable far below the resonance frequency, with heating only occurring slowly, suggesting a prethermal Floquet CSL phase in the thermodynamic limit controlled by local energy scales.
AI.motivation: To understand whether a topologically ordered chiral spin liquid can survive under periodic driving (Floquet dynamics), and to identify the mechanism controlling its stability and heating.
AI.method: Exact computation of the one-period propagator in all symmetry sectors of the 4×4 torus; analysis of quasienergy spectrum, time-averaged energy, and stroboscopic time evolution; comparison with chiral PEPS tensor for the static problem.
AI.result: The topological doublet remains the isolated bottom of the Floquet spectrum down to ω≈6J1, far below the resonance frequency ω_res≈11.5J1. Quasienergy crossings are parametrically weak avoided crossings invisible in average energy. Heating is absent for ω≳ω_res and slow below.
AI.conclusion: Stability is controlled by local energy scales, not the many-body bandwidth, implying a prethermal Floquet CSL exists in the thermodynamic limit with exponentially long heating times in ω/J1.

title: Glauber dynamics phase transitions in athermal random field Blume-Capel and Blume-Emery-Grifitths models
summary: We solve the two models for Glauber dynamics and in equilibrium, both in the presence and absence of the external magnetic field on a complete graph. We compare the steady state of the Glauber dynamics with equilibrium and find that for low values of variance $R$ of the Gaussian random field, the steady state of the Glauber dynamics depends on the initial state. Beyond a critical value $R_{c}$ the equilibrium and non equilibrium steady states coincide. The variance $R$ in random field models behaves similar to the temperature. The location of both the continuous and first order transitions can be obtained exactly for the Glauber dynamics steady state. The frustration is introduced by considering repulsive bi-quadratic interaction for Blume-Emery-Griffiths model. We also. consider repulsive bi-quadratic interaction and show that $R_c$ can become zero depending on the value of the crystal field. Interestingly, we also find that even when a system has $R_c=0$ at the start of quasi-static evolution with Glauber dynamics, with increasing $R$, in some regime of the couplings, the model undergoes a crossover to a random field Ising model universaility with $R_c$ changing from $0$ to $\sqrt{\frac{2}π}$. In the presence of uniform magnetic field, regions of first order transition exhibit hysteresis under Glauber dynamics. These models exhibit rectangular, hexagonal, parallelogram, wasp-waisted, and double hysteresis loops. We derive the shapes of hysteresis loops analytically giving the equation for the value of the coercive field and show that while the area under the hysteresis loop depends on $R$, the shape is determined by the behavior of the models at $R=0$. In particular, in the case of Blume-Emery-Griffiths model the hysteresis plots have regions of continuous and first order transitions both, resulting in a rich phase diagram that depends non-trivially on the initial state.

AI.tldr: This paper solves Glauber dynamics and equilibrium models for random field systems on a complete graph, showing that the steady state depends on initial conditions below a critical variance $R_c$, beyond which equilibrium and non-equilibrium states coincide. It examines frustration via repulsive bi-quadratic interactions, crossover behavior, hysteresis loops (rectangular, hexagonal, etc.), and derives coercive field equations, revealing rich phase diagrams dependent on initial states.
AI.motivation: To understand the relationship between Glauber dynamics (non-equilibrium steady states) and equilibrium in random field models, particularly how frustration, magnetic fields, and initial conditions affect phase transitions and hysteresis.
AI.method: Exact solution of Glauber dynamics and equilibrium on a complete graph for random field Ising and Blume-Emery-Griffiths models, with and without external magnetic fields and repulsive bi-quadratic interactions.
AI.result: (1) Below critical $R_c$, steady state depends on initial state; above $R_c$, equilibrium and non-equilibrium coincide. (2) $R_c$ can vanish depending on crystal field. (3) Systems with $R_c=0$ can cross over to random field Ising universality ($R_c=\sqrt{2/\pi}$).
