title: Symmetry-Based Microscopic Theory of the Unconventional Pairing Mechanism in La$_5$Ni$_3$O$_{11}$
summary: Recent experiments report high-temperature superconductivity in the hybrid nickelate $\mathrm{La}_5\mathrm{Ni}_3\mathrm{O}_{11}$, which is composed of alternating stacks of bilayer $\mathrm{La}_3\mathrm{Ni}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ and monolayer $\mathrm{La}_2\mathrm{NiO}_4$. However, the superconducting transition temperature $T_c \approx 64~\mathrm{K}$ for $\mathrm{La}_5\mathrm{Ni}_3\mathrm{O}_{11}$ is remarkably lower than the $80~\mathrm{K}$ observed for pressurized $\mathrm{La}_3\mathrm{Ni}_2\mathrm{O}_7$. Thus, an unified microscopic theory is required to address the difference in the pairing mechanisms between these systems. Here, we develop a phenomenological symmetry-based approach to systematically analyze the low-energy physics in $\mathrm{La}_5\mathrm{Ni}_3\mathrm{O}_{11}$, which is obtained by a charge self-consistent density functional theory plus dynamical mean-field theory method. We show that the superconductivity in $\mathrm{La}_5\mathrm{Ni}_3\mathrm{O}_{11}$ exhibits a two-gap nature, consisting of a leading interlayer pairing between the $d_{z^2}$ orbitals and a subleading intralayer pairing between the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbitals. The reduction of $T_c$ can be attributed to the diminished contribution of the interlayer pairing, as reflected by the hopping parameter ratio $|t_{\perp}^z/t_{\parallel}^{x}|$. Base on this unified picture, we discuss the possible pairing mechanism and the role of $γ$ pocket for the superconductivity in the bilayer NiO$_2$ planes of nickelate superconductors.

AI.motivation: To resolve the puzzling difference in superconducting transition temperatures between the hybrid nickelate La₅Ni₃O₁₁ (Tc ≈ 64 K) and pressurized bilayer La₃Ni₂O₇ (Tc ≈ 80 K), and to provide a unified microscopic theory for the pairing mechanisms in these nickelate superconductors.
AI.method: A phenomenological symmetry-based approach combined with charge self-consistent DFT + dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to analyze the low-energy physics of La₅Ni₃O₁₁, which consists of alternating bilayer La₃Ni₂O₇ and monolayer La₂NiO₄ stacks.

The reduced Tc (64 K vs. 80 K) is attributed to diminished interlayer pairing contribution, quantified by the hopping parameter ratio |t⊥^z / t∥^x|.
AI.conclusion: The unified picture explains the Tc difference via interlayer coupling strength, discusses the pairing mechanism and the role of the γ pocket in bilayer NiO₂ planes of nickelate superconductors.

title: Phonon dynamics in Chromium under pressure: absence of phonon criticality at the approach of the quantum critical point
summary: Fermi surface nesting is key to understanding the origin of the itinerant antiferromagnetic spin density wave in Chromium. At very low temperature, this density wave is destroyed above the critical pressure $P_c\approx$10~GPa, defining a quantum critical point. Strong electron-phonon coupling induces a small phonon softening close to the $H-$point of the Brillouin zone as well as close to the $H$-point. These phonon anomalies are known as Kohn anomalies. They remain unchanged down to 50K and are known to be present in both the paramagnetic and the antiferromagnetic phases. This paper presents inelastic X-ray scattering experiments on the phonon dispersion curves under pressure, up to $P=$15.6~GPa far above the critical pressure $P_c$. The softening of the well-known phonon anomalies is still present which leads to conclude that they do not play a major role at the antiferromagnetic ordering. Based on ab-initio calculation, the robustness of the Fermi surface nesting under pressure, explain the presence of these Kohn anomalies above the critical pressure.

AI.tldr: This paper uses inelastic X-ray scattering and ab-initio calculations to show that Kohn anomalies (phonon softenings) in Chromium persist far above the critical pressure P_c≈10 GPa where the antiferromagnetic spin density wave is destroyed. The robustness of Fermi surface nesting under pressure explains why these phonon anomalies remain unchanged, indicating they do not play a major role in the antiferromagnetic ordering.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the phonon anomalies (Kohn anomalies) observed in Chromium are fundamentally linked to the antiferromagnetic spin density wave ordering, by examining their behavior under high pressure above the quantum critical point.
AI.method: Inelastic X-ray scattering experiments on phonon dispersion curves under high pressure (up to 15.6 GPa, above P_c≈10 GPa), combined with ab-initio calculations.
AI.result: The phonon softening anomalies persist unchanged far above the critical pressure where antiferromagnetic ordering vanishes, and ab-initio calculations show that Fermi surface nesting remains robust under pressure.
AI.conclusion: The Kohn anomalies do not play a major role in the antiferromagnetic ordering of Chromium; their persistence above P_c is explained by the robustness of Fermi surface nesting under pressure.

title: A Unified Discrete and Continuous Theory of Core-Halo Complexity Maximizers
summary: The maximization of statistical complexity has long been associated with the emergence of probability distributions lying between perfect order and complete disorder. While previous studies have shown that complexity-maximizing distributions exhibit a two-level structure in finite discrete systems, an analogous unified treatment for both discrete and continuous probability spaces has remained unavailable. In this work, we develop a general variational framework for a generalized statistical complexity constructed from Shannon and Renyi entropies. We derive a common stationary equation governing both discrete probability masses and continuous probability densities and prove that every stationary solution necessarily possesses exactly two probability levels, establishing a universal core-halo structure. We further demonstrate that the optimization problem reduces to a single multiplicity parameter and prove that the global complexity maximum is attained by the smallest admissible core, corresponding to a single dominant state in the discrete case and an infinitesimal core in the continuous limit. These results provide a complete analytical characterization of the complexity-maximizing distributions and reveal a common mathematical structure underlying complexity optimization in both discrete and continuous settings. The framework establishes a unified foundation for generalized statistical complexity with potential applications in statistical mechanics, information theory, and the analysis of complex systems.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a unified variational framework for maximizing statistical complexity using Shannon and Renyi entropies, proving that all stationary solutions exhibit a two-level (core-halo) structure in both discrete and continuous probability spaces, with the global maximum achieved by the smallest admissible core.
AI.motivation: Previous work showed complexity-maximizing distributions have a two-level structure in finite discrete systems, but no unified treatment existed for both discrete and continuous probability spaces.
AI.method: The authors develop a general variational framework for a generalized statistical complexity constructed from Shannon and Renyi entropies, derive a common stationary equation governing both discrete masses and continuous densities, and reduce the optimization to a single multiplicity parameter.
AI.result: Every stationary solution possesses exactly two probability levels (universal core-halo structure); the global complexity maximum is attained by the smallest admissible core — a single dominant state in discrete case and an infinitesimal core in the continuous limit.
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes a unified foundation for generalized statistical complexity with applications in statistical mechanics, information theory, and complex systems analysis.

title: Beyond Janus Atomic Ordering: High-Throughput First-Principles Search for Hidden MoSO Monolayer Structures
summary: Despite the growing interest in two-dimensional (2D) MoSO systems, existing studies have exclusively focused on conventional Janus structures. In this work, we perform high-throughput first-principles calculations to explore novel stable 2D MoSO monolayers. Combined with random sampling strategy, graph theory and group theory, we successfully screen out three novel non-Janus 2D MoSO monolayers from 1325 candidate structures, namely Reversed 2H-MoSO, Hybrid 2H-MoSO, and Hybrid 1T'-MoSO. Compared with Janus MoSO monolayers, the non-Janus MoSO counterparts possess lower binding energies, varying from -4.38 to -4.51 eV/atom. A systematic combination of dynamic, thermodynamic, and mechanical stability analyses corroborates their excellent structural robustness. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations confirm their superior thermal resistance, with the structures remaining stable at temperatures beyond 2000 K. Interestingly, unlike the semiconducting Janus MoSO, the Hybrid 1T'-MoSO monolayer exhibits distinct metallic characteristics. Furthermore, we found that strain and curvature can enable controlled phase transitions of MoSO among semiconducting, semimetallic, and metallic phases. More importantly, the Hybrid 1T'-MoSO exhibits favorable HER activity with a Gibbs free energy of -0.002 eV, rendering it a promising candidate for hydrogen evolution catalysis. This work not only expands the family of 2D MoSO materials but also provides a reliable strategy for discovering stable functional 2D materials via high-throughput computation.

AI.tldr: High-throughput first-principles calculations identify three novel non-Janus 2D MoSO monolayers (Reversed 2H-MoSO, Hybrid 2H-MoSO, Hybrid 1T'-MoSO) from 1325 candidates, exhibiting lower binding energies, stability beyond 2000 K, strain/curvature-controlled phase transitions, and excellent HER catalytic activity (Gibbs free energy of -0.002 eV for Hybrid 1T'-MoSO).
AI.motivation: Existing studies on 2D MoSO systems have exclusively focused on conventional Janus structures, leaving the broader structural landscape unexplored.
AI.method: High-throughput first-principles calculations combined with random sampling strategy, graph theory, and group theory to screen 1325 candidate structures.
AI.result: Three novel non-Janus 2D MoSO monolayers discovered: Reversed 2H-MoSO, Hybrid 2H-MoSO, and Hybrid 1T'-MoSO. They have lower binding energies (-4.38 to -4.51 eV/atom), stability beyond 2000 K, and Hybrid 1T'-MoSO exhibits metallic characteristics and superior HER activity (Gibbs free energy of -0.002 eV).
AI.conclusion: This work expands the 2D MoSO material family and provides a reliable high-throughput computation strategy for discovering stable functional 2D materials.

title: Study of ordering in (MoCrTi)$_{100-x}$Al$_x$ refractory high-entropy alloys using machine learning interatomic potential
summary: Refractory high-entropy alloys have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature applications due to their exceptional mechanical properties. Understanding the thermodynamic mechanisms underlying chemical ordering in these complex systems is critical for optimizing their performance. In this work, by utilizing a universal machine learning interatomic potential with hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations, the temperature-dependent thermodynamics and mechanical properties of (MoCrTi)(100-x)Alx system have been investigated. The heat capacities and short-range order parameters reveal distinct order-disorder transition behaviors. While the Mo25Cr25Ti25Al25 and Mo32Cr32Ti32Al4 alloys exhibit a single transition dominated by the synergistic ordering of B2-type atomic pairs, the Mo28Cr28Ti28Al16 and Mo30Cr30Ti30Al10 alloys display two separate transitions: a low-temperature stage driven by specific pairs (Mo-Al in Mo28Cr28Ti28Al16; Al-Al in Mo30Cr30Ti30Al10) and a high-temperature stage governed by the remaining pairs. Structural analysis indicates that in the low-temperature ordered B2 phase, Mo and Al share one sublattice while Cr and Ti share the other. Furthermore, the relationship between ordering and mechanical stiffness has been identified. Ordering significantly enhances the elastic constants and moduli, and gives rise to a non-monotonic compositional dependence. Unlike random solid solutions, where stiffness increases monotonically with decreasing Al content, ordered configurations exhibit a non-monotonic trend, peaking at the Mo30Cr30Ti30Al10 alloy. This enhancement is attributed to an optimized population of stiff atomic pairs induced by strong short-range order. These findings provide fundamental insights into the interplay between compositions, chemical ordering, and mechanical performance, offering guidance for the design of refractory high-entropy alloys.

AI.tldr: Using machine learning interatomic potentials and hybrid Monte Carlo/MD simulations, this study investigates temperature-dependent thermodynamics and mechanical properties of (MoCrTi)(100-x)Alx refractory high-entropy alloys, revealing distinct order-disorder transitions and ordering-enhanced, non-monotonic mechanical stiffness.
AI.motivation: Understanding thermodynamic mechanisms of chemical ordering in refractory high-entropy alloys is critical for optimizing their high-temperature performance.
AI.method: Universal machine learning interatomic potential combined with hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.result: Mo25Cr25Ti25Al25 and Mo32Cr32Ti32Al4 show a single B2-type order-disorder transition; Mo28Cr28Ti28Al16 and Mo30Cr30Ti30Al10 show two separate transitions. Ordering enhances elastic constants/moduli and produces non-monotonic compositional dependence, peaking at Mo30Cr30Ti30Al10 rather than the monotonic trend seen in random solid solutions.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide fundamental insights into the interplay between compositions, chemical ordering, and mechanical performance, offering guidance for designing refractory high-entropy alloys.

title: DFT+U+V is equivalent to DFT+U with density-dependent hybridized projectors
comment: 8 pages with an additional 6 pages of supplemental material
summary: Hubbard-corrected density-functional theory (DFT+$U$) is a popular tool for first-principles modeling of materials with localized $d$ or $f$ electrons, but its on-site corrections tend to over-localize charge and break covalent bonds. Inter-site $+V$ corrections were introduced to counter this and are now widely used, but a formal justification has been lacking. Here we show that -- to first order in $V/U$ -- inter-site corrections are exactly equivalent to on-site DFT+$U$ evaluated on a density-dependent redefinition of the Hubbard projectors, hybridized with those of neighboring sites, providing insight into the explicit mechanism by which $V$ affects covalency. If the projectors are held frozen, as is common practice, the equivalence partially breaks down. Beyond reinterpreting the formalism, these results sharpen the questions of how $V$ should be computed and what the Hubbard subspaces fundamentally are.

AI.tldr: DFT+$U$ with inter-site $+V$ corrections is shown to be equivalent (to first order in $V/U$) to on-site DFT+$U$ using density-dependent, hybridized Hubbard projectors, revealing how $V$ affects covalency; frozen projectors partially break this equivalence, raising questions about computing $V$ and defining Hubbard subspaces.
AI.motivation: Inter-site $+V$ corrections in DFT+$U$ are widely used to counter the over-localization and bond-breaking caused by on-site corrections, but a formal theoretical justification for their mechanism has been lacking.
AI.method: Analytical derivation showing that inter-site corrections are equivalent to on-site DFT+$U$ evaluated on a density-dependent redefinition of Hubbard projectors hybridized with neighboring sites, to first order in $V/U$.
AI.result: The equivalence provides an explicit mechanism for how $V$ affects covalency; if projectors are held frozen (common practice), the equivalence partially breaks down.
AI.conclusion: These results sharpen fundamental questions about how $V$ should be computed and what the Hubbard subspaces fundamentally are.

title: Planar Microcavities can Suppress Exciplex Formation and Increase the Emission Efficiency of Organic Semiconductors
summary: Optical microcavities are widely used to control the emission of organic semiconductors, but their ability to reshape the molecular pathways that precede emission remains largely unexplored. Here we show that embedding a ZnPc:TPBi blend in a planar Fabry-Pérot microcavity suppresses the formation of non-radiative exciplexes and removes bimolecular annihilation at high excitation densities, increasing the photoluminescence quantum yield by more than forty-fold under continuous-wave excitation. This enhancement is far larger than expected from the weak Purcell effect. Instead, transient spectroscopy, power-dependent photoluminescence and kinetic modelling point to a cavity-induced rebalancing of excited-state populations: long-range Förster energy transfer from ZnPc monomers to emissive aggregates is enhanced, allowing it to outcompete charge transfer to dark exciplexes. Electromagnetic calculations predict FRET enhancements of up to ~400-fold at relevant distances, consistent with the observed suppression of exciplex-mediated losses. Our results show that optical cavities can control not only how molecules emit, but also which excited states they form, opening a route to improved efficiency and reduced roll-off in organic optoelectronic and photonic devices.

AI.tldr: Embedding a ZnPc:TPBi blend in a Fabry-Pérot microcavity suppresses non-radiative exciplex formation and bimolecular annihilation, increasing photoluminescence quantum yield >40-fold under CW excitation via cavity-enhanced Förster energy transfer that outcompetes charge transfer to dark states.
AI.motivation: To explore whether optical microcavities can reshape molecular excited-state pathways beyond controlling emission, specifically by suppressing non-radiative loss channels in organic semiconductors.
AI.method: ZnPc:TPBi blend embedded in a planar Fabry-Pérot microcavity; characterized by transient spectroscopy, power-dependent photoluminescence, kinetic modelling, and electromagnetic calculations of FRET enhancement.
AI.result: >40-fold photoluminescence quantum yield enhancement under CW excitation; suppression of exciplex formation and bimolecular annihilation; FRET enhancement up to ~400-fold at relevant distances, consistent with exciplex-mediated loss suppression.
AI.conclusion: Optical cavities can control which excited states molecules form, not just how they emit, offering a route to improved efficiency and reduced roll-off in organic optoelectronic and photonic devices.

title: Structural and Vibrational Properties of D$_3$Se from First Principles: Anharmonic Quantum and Isotope Effects
summary: Hydrogen-rich superconductors have garnered considerable interest following the discovery of hot superconductivity in high pressure H$_3$S, reviving prospects for room temperature superconductors under high-pressures. Using H$_3$Se as a reference system, we investigate the vibrational and superconducting properties of D$_3$Se in the Im\bar{3}m phase across 60-200 GPa by combining first-principles calculations with the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation to treat ionic quantum and anharmonic effects. These effects introduce significant renormalization to the phonon spectra and stabilize the lattice down to at least 70 GPa, well below the harmonic prediction of >110 GPa. Ultimately, the phonon renormalizations alter the electron-phonon coupling, introducing a decrease in the superconducting critical temperature by about 3-16 K across the studied pressure range with respect to standard calculations. Including anharmonic phonons within the Migdal-Eliashberg theory yields $T_c \approx 154$ K at 75 GPa (with $μ^* = 0.1$, $λ = 3.0$), highlighting D3Se as a promising high-Tc superconductor at moderate pressures. Examining the role of anharmonicity in the isotope effect, we find that at 200 GPa it suppresses the isotope coefficient $α$ to 0.29 one third below the harmonic value (0.44) which approaches the BCS limit of 0.5. This dramatic reduction demonstrates that anharmonicity fundamentally governs the isotope effect on this system. The stark discrepancy between anharmonic and harmonic descriptions underscores the need for targeted experimental efforts to resolve the origin of the persistent theory-experiment discrepancy in compressed hydrides.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates D₃Se (deuterated H₃Se) under high pressure, showing that anharmonic and quantum ionic effects significantly impact phonon spectra, stabilize the structure to lower pressures, reduce superconducting Tc by 3-16 K, and suppress the isotope coefficient α from 0.44 to 0.29, with a predicted Tc ≈ 154 K at 75 GPa.
AI.motivation: Following the discovery of hot superconductivity in high-pressure H₃S, hydrogen-rich superconductors have revived prospects for room-temperature superconductivity. However, persistent theory-experiment discrepancies in compressed hydrides remain unresolved, motivating a study of anharmonic and quantum ionic effects in these systems using H₃Se/D₃Se as a reference.
AI.method: First-principles calculations combined with the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA) to treat ionic quantum and anharmonic effects, applied to D₃Se in the Im3̄m phase across 60-200 GPa. Superconducting properties are evaluated within Migdal-Eliashberg theory.

Tc decreases by about 3-16 K across the pressure range; predicted Tc ≈ 154 K at 75 GPa (μ* = 0.1, λ = 3.0). The isotope coefficient α is suppressed from 0.44 (harmonic) to 0.29 at 200 GPa, one third below the BCS limit of 0.5.

title: Universal Dynamic Scaling of 2D Quantum Ising Transition on the Fuzzy Sphere
comment: 4.5 pages with 4 figures in main text + 1.5 pages of appendix
summary: We revisit the problem of \textit{real-time} quantum dynamics of the paradigmatic two dimensional transverse-field Ising model using the recently developed fuzzy sphere regularization scheme. By linearly ramping the transverse field from the paramagnetic phase to criticality, we study the finite-time scaling behavior of the squared order parameter $\langle m_z^2 \rangle$, the excitation energy density $Q$, and the two-point correlation function of $m_z$. We establish numerically that, at intermediate quench rate, $\langle m_z^2 \rangle$ follows the conventional Kibble-Zurek prediction set by the critical exponents of the $3$D Ising universality class, and the correlation function exhibits the expected exponential decay whose correlation length can be used to estimate the non-universal scaling coefficient in the freeze-out time/length. In contrast, the excitation energy density $Q$ does not reach the same scaling regime at available system sizes due to large effective finite-size gap from symmetry-enforced level sparsity in the energy spectrum. At slow quench rates the universal quasi-adiabatic scaling for both $\langle m_z^2 \rangle$ and $Q$ is recovered. Since the fuzzy sphere construction can realize not only the Ising conformal field theory (CFT), but a broad family of $(2+1)d$ CFTs, our results establish a route to the real-time critical dynamics of strongly coupled CFTs that are otherwise computationally challenging to study.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the fuzzy sphere regularization scheme to study real-time quantum dynamics of the 2D transverse-field Ising model, finding that the squared order parameter and correlation function follow Kibble-Zurek scaling predictions of the 3D Ising universality class, while excitation energy density exhibits different behavior due to finite-size effects. This approach can be extended to other (2+1)d CFTs.
AI.motivation: To study real-time quantum dynamics of strongly coupled CFTs, which are computationally challenging, using the fuzzy sphere regularization scheme as a new route.
AI.method: Using fuzzy sphere regularization to linearly ramp the transverse field from paramagnetic phase to criticality, then analyzing finite-time scaling of squared order parameter, excitation energy density, and two-point correlation function.
AI.result: At intermediate quench rates, ⟨m_z²⟩ follows Kibble-Zurek scaling from 3D Ising universality class, and correlation functions show exponential decay with extractable correlation length. Excitation energy density Q does not reach the same scaling regime at available system sizes due to large finite-size gap from symmetry-enforced level sparsity. At slow quench rates, universal quasi-adiabatic scaling is recovered.
AI.conclusion: The fuzzy sphere regularization provides a viable route to study real-time critical dynamics of (2+1)d CFTs, not limited to the Ising model, enabling exploration of strongly coupled CFTs that are otherwise computationally difficult.

title: Large scale behavior in the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation: The Schwinger-Dyson route
summary: The present paper is a study of the large scale properties of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. By using a Schwinger-Dyson framework, we aim to provide a proof that the only solutions that can sustain a stable scaling in the infrared limit have a negative effective viscosity (in the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky sense) with a minimal set of hypotheses, thereby showing that this constitutes a general property of the wave equation that does not depend on a specific set of truncations of a renormalisation group flow, or limitations of a given numerical scheme for example.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the large-scale properties of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation using a Schwinger-Dyson framework, proving that stable scaling solutions in the infrared limit must have negative effective viscosity, establishing this as a general property independent of specific truncations or numerical schemes.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous proof that negative effective viscosity in the infrared limit is a general property of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, not contingent on specific renormalisation group truncations or numerical schemes.
AI.method: A Schwinger-Dyson framework is employed to analyze the large-scale properties of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation under a minimal set of hypotheses.
AI.result: The only solutions that sustain stable scaling in the infrared limit have negative effective viscosity (in the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky sense).
AI.conclusion: Negative effective viscosity is a universal, scheme-independent property of the wave equation at large scales, not an artifact of specific computational or renormalisation approaches.

title: A field theory approach to Breit-type Hamiltonians in gapped Dirac systems
summary: We develop a path-integral-based field theory for deriving Breit-type low-energy Hamiltonians for gapped Dirac systems coupled to both vector and axial gauge fields. Treating the mass gap as the large energy scale, we integrate out the high-energy component of the Dirac spinor and obtain a canonical Schrödinger description for the remaining low-energy degrees of freedom. For the ordinary Dirac equation, our method reproduces the conventional Breit Hamiltonian order by order. In the presence of axial gauge fields, however, the resulting Hamiltonian contains additional vector-axial couplings that have no analogue in the traditional electromagnetic case. We illustrate the method using three- and two-dimensional Dirac models and discuss its relevance to gapped Weyl systems, where dynamical axial fields can generate distinctive low-energy transport signatures.

By integrating out high-energy components, it reproduces conventional Breit Hamiltonians for ordinary Dirac equations but reveals new vector-axial couplings absent in standard electromagnetism when axial gauge fields are present. The method is illustrated for 3D and 2D Dirac models, with relevance to gapped Weyl systems where dynamical axial fields yield distinctive low-energy transport signatures.
AI.motivation: To extend the Breit-type Hamiltonian derivation to Dirac systems coupled to both vector and axial gauge fields, going beyond standard electromagnetic cases to capture new physics arising from axial couplings (e.g., in gapped Weyl systems).
AI.method: A path-integral-based field theory approach treating the mass gap as a large energy scale, integrating out high-energy Dirac spinor components to obtain a canonical Schrödinger description for the low-energy degrees of freedom.
AI.result: For ordinary Dirac equations, the method reproduces conventional Breit Hamiltonians order by order. For systems with axial gauge fields, additional vector-axial couplings emerge that have no electromagnetic analogue.
AI.conclusion: The method is applicable to 3D and 2D Dirac models and is relevant for gapped Weyl systems, where dynamical axial fields produce unique low-energy transport signatures not found in conventional electromagnetic systems.

title: Superconductivity in MgHCu3 perovskite revisited
comment: 13 pages, 3 Figures, 1 Table, and Supplementary Information of 9 pages
summary: We reexamine the crystal structure, electronic structure, lattice dynamics, phonon dispersion, electron-phonon coupling, and superconducting properties of MgHCu3 perovskite using the PBEsol and PBE functionals. This perovskite phase was recently proposed to exhibit superconductivity with the critical superconducting temperature, TC, of 42 K, which falls slightly over the classical 40 K limit for the phonon driven superconductivity. We show that although the crystal and electronic structure of this hypothetical compound are quite robust with respect to the k point mesh and functional used, yet the phonons and phonon related properties are extremely sensitive to the density of the grid chosen as well as functional used for calculations. Correspondingly, the values of the critical superconducting temperature calculated here for different Gaussian broadenings vary in a broad range of ca. 10 to 31 K and they do not exceed the classical limit. We suggest that the properties of this and many other high TC hydrides claimed should be thoroughly scrutinized using a variety of functionals, and benchmarked with experiment, to provide more reliable values of TC.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines the MgHCu3 perovskite superconductor and finds that while its crystal and electronic structures are robust, its phonon properties and predicted superconducting critical temperature (TC) are highly sensitive to computational parameters (k-point mesh, functional, Gaussian broadening). The calculated TC ranges from ~10 to 31 K, below the classical 40 K limit, contradicting the previously claimed 42 K.
AI.motivation: To scrutinize the previously reported high TC (42 K) of MgHCu3 perovskite, which exceeds the classical phonon-mediated superconductivity limit (40 K), by testing the robustness of computational predictions under different functionals and numerical parameters.
AI.method: DFT calculations using PBEsol and PBE functionals with varying k-point meshes and Gaussian broadenings to compute crystal structure, electronic structure, lattice dynamics, phonon dispersion, electron-phonon coupling, and superconducting TC.
AI.result: Crystal and electronic structures are robust across functionals and grids, but phonon properties and TC are extremely sensitive to computational parameters. TC ranges broadly from ~10 to 31 K depending on Gaussian broadening, never exceeding the 40 K classical limit.
AI.conclusion: Previously claimed high TC of 42 K for MgHCu3 is not reproducible; such hydride superconductors require thorough scrutiny with multiple functionals and experimental benchmarking to obtain reliable TC values.

title: Color superconductors and holon metals from doping a Fractional Chern insulator
summary: We develop a unified framework for metallic and superconducting phases obtained by doping a fractional Chern insulator (FCI) with $C=1/3$. Starting from the parton construction $c(\mathbf r)=f_1(\mathbf r)f_2(\mathbf r)f_3(\mathbf r)$, the low-energy theory has $SU(3)_{\mathrm{gauge}}\times SU(3)_{\mathrm{valley}}$ symmetry and nine Fermi pockets formed by charge-$-e/3$ holons $ψ_{ab}$, where $a$ and $b$ label color and valley. Viewing the holons as quarks connects this problem to color superconductivity in high-energy physics. Color-antisymmetric pairing produces a class of charge-$2e$ superconductors with angular momentum $L=3n$ and chiral central charge $c_-=m/2$, where $m$ is odd. Thus a gas of charge-$e/3$ anyons can enter a superconducting phase directly without binding. Particle--hole color--valley Higgs fields instead produce two $Z_3$ orthogonal metals with one or three pockets, transforming respectively as a singlet or triplet of $SU(3)_{\mathrm{valley}}$. A $U(1)^2$ holon metal with three identical pockets can preserve the triangular-lattice space group while reducing the emergent valley symmetry down to $S_3$. Its pairing instabilities include a gapped charge $2e$ $f-if$ superconductor and a gapless charge-$2e$ orthogonal superconductor with $\langle cc\rangle=0$ and a Bogoliubov Fermi surface at $Γ$. Finally, we discuss the possibility of a chemical-potential-tuned transition from the FCI to superconductivity and argue that all nine fermions may be required if the transition preserves the full emergent $SU(3)_v$ symmetry.

AI.tldr: A unified framework for metallic and superconducting phases from doping a C=1/3 fractional Chern insulator is developed using parton construction, revealing SU(3)gauge × SU(3)valley symmetry, nine Fermi pockets of charge-e/3 holons, and connections to color superconductivity, yielding various superconducting and orthogonal metal phases.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified theoretical framework connecting fractional Chern insulator (FCI) states to metallic and superconducting phases upon doping, using parton construction to reveal the underlying symmetry and topological structure.
AI.method: Employ parton construction c(r)=f1(r)f2(r)f3(r) to decompose electron into three partons, analyze SU(3)gauge × SU(3)valley symmetry, and classify pairing and Higgs-channel instabilities of the nine holon (charge -e/3) Fermi pockets.
AI.result: Identified color-antisymmetric pairing yields charge-2e superconductors (L=3n, c-=m/2); particle-hole color-valley Higgs fields produce Z3 orthogonal metals; U(1)^2 holon metal with three pockets leads to gapped f-if superconductor and gapless orthogonal superconductor with Bogoliubov Fermi surface.
AI.conclusion: Charge-e/3 anyons can directly enter a superconducting phase without binding, and the FCI-to-superconductor transition may require all nine fermions to preserve the full emergent SU(3)v symmetry.

title: Expansion of a free Fermi gas released from an isotropic trapping potential
summary: We consider a system of non-interacting fermions prepared in the many-body ground state of an isotropic trapping potential in any dimension, and investigate the ballistic expansion of the fermionic cloud after the potential is suddenly released. Using semi-classical techniques, we derive the full late-time profile of the expanding cloud in the regime when the fermion number is large. We thus obtain explicit expressions for power-law potentials with arbitrary exponent $a$ and in all dimensions $d$. The momentum distribution and the spatial profile of the cloud exhibit a universal edge exponent $d/a$, thus generalizing the Wigner semi-circle law and the Thomas-Fermi distribution.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the ballistic expansion of non-interacting fermions from an isotropic trap after sudden release, deriving late-time spatial profiles using semi-classical methods for large fermion numbers, with results showing a universal edge exponent d/a for power-law potentials.
AI.motivation: To understand the ballistic expansion dynamics of fermionic clouds after trap release, generalizing known results (Wigner semi-circle law, Thomas-Fermi distribution) to arbitrary power-law potentials and dimensions.
AI.method: Semi-classical techniques are applied to analyze the many-body ground state of non-interacting fermions in an isotropic trapping potential, then the ballistic expansion after sudden potential release is investigated in the large-fermion-number regime.
AI.result: Explicit late-time profile expressions are derived for power-law potentials with exponent a in any dimension d. The momentum distribution and spatial profile exhibit a universal edge exponent d/a, generalizing the Wigner semi-circle law and Thomas-Fermi distribution.
AI.conclusion: The ballistic expansion of non-interacting fermions from isotropic traps yields universal scaling behavior governed by the exponent d/a, providing a generalized framework beyond standard results.

title: Three Million Years Opposite State Data Retention in Partially Switched Wurtzite Ferroelectrics
summary: Ferroelectric memories based on the wurtzite-structured ferroelectrics are projected to store information for more than 3 million years at 150C. These results are extracted by combining standard domain wall motion limited switching kinetics with the near-by-electrode injection model for opposite state retention in ferroelectric random access memory. This impressive performance is greatly aided by switching only a fraction of the total polarization to store data, in order to limit the initial imprint variation of the devices - an effect that is universally observed in films with different thicknesses (60 nm - 270 nm) and different compounds (AlScN and AlScBN). Paradoxically, yet systematically, this reduction in initial imprint consistently results in larger switching polarization after a given time, compared to the fully switching state and 5-7 orders of magnitude improved opposite state retention. Finally, partial switching is able to simultaneously boost endurance against premature polarization loss and breakdown, making it a promising strategy for improved operation of ferroelectric devices with large spontaneous polarization, in particularly wurtzite-structured compounds.

AI.tldr: Partial switching in wurtzite-structured ferroelectric memories enables over 3 million years of data retention at 150°C, reduced imprint variation, 5-7 orders of magnitude improved retention, and enhanced endurance against polarization loss and breakdown.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that partial switching—rather than full polarization switching—can dramatically improve retention, endurance, and reliability in wurtzite-structured ferroelectric memories (e.g., AlScN, AlScBN) by mitigating initial imprint variation.
AI.method: Combined standard domain wall motion limited switching kinetics with a near-by-electrode injection model for opposite-state retention. Experimental data were collected across films of varying thicknesses (60–270 nm) and compounds (AlScN, AlScBN).
AI.result: Partial switching yields 5–7 orders of magnitude better opposite-state retention, larger switching polarization after a given time compared to full switching, and projected data retention exceeding 3 million years at 150°C. It also improves endurance against premature polarization loss and breakdown.
AI.conclusion: Partial switching is a promising strategy for improving the operation of ferroelectric devices with large spontaneous polarization, particularly wurtzite-structured compounds, by simultaneously boosting retention and endurance.

title: Symmetry-isolated magnetoelectric electro-optic effects in noncentrosymmetric metals
summary: We classify the symmetry-constrained forms of the Berry curvature dipole $\mathbf{D}$, gyrotropic magnetic tensor $\mathbf{K}$, and magnetoelectric electro-optic (EO) tensor $\mathbf{G}$, which describe metallic optical and EO effects in time-reversal symmetric, noncentrosymmetric metals. We identify 11 space groups (SGs) in which $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ vanish by symmetry while $\mathbf{G}$ remains allowed, thereby providing a more direct route to observing the recently predicted magnetoelectric EO effects associated with $\mathbf{G}$. First-principles based calculations confirm that $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ vanish for representative materials, while $\mathbf{G}$ remains allowed and tunable via Fermi level shifting. We further show that the choices of SG and experimental configuration provide complementary paths for isolating $\mathbf{G}$-driven EO effects, including cases where $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ are also symmetry-allowed. In an oblique-incidence geometry, the $\mathbf{D}$-driven response produces a helicity-even absorption or gain correction, whereas the $\mathbf{G}$-driven response couples the $s$ and $p$ optical sectors and produces a bias-induced circular dichroism with a characteristic $\sinθ\cosθ$ angular dependence. This provides a direct experimental route for separating the $\mathbf{D}$- and $\mathbf{G}$-driven EO signatures in noncentrosymmetric metals.

AI.tldr: This paper classifies symmetry constraints on Berry curvature dipole (D), gyrotropic magnetic tensor (K), and magnetoelectric electro-optic tensor (G) in noncentrosymmetric metals, identifies 11 space groups where D and K vanish but G remains, and proposes experimental configurations to isolate G-driven electro-optic effects via oblique-incidence geometry with characteristic angular dependence.
AI.motivation: To provide a more direct route for observing the recently predicted magnetoelectric electro-optic effects associated with the tensor G by identifying symmetry conditions where competing D and K tensors vanish, and to develop experimental methods for separating D-driven and G-driven electro-optic signatures in noncentrosymmetric metals.
AI.method: Symmetry classification of tensors D, K, and G across space groups; first-principles DFT calculations on representative materials; analysis of oblique-incidence optical geometry to distinguish D-driven (helicity-even) and G-driven (s-p coupling, bias-induced circular dichroism with sinθcosθ angular dependence) responses.
AI.result: Identified 11 space groups where D and K vanish by symmetry while G remains allowed; first-principles calculations confirm vanishing D and K with tunable G via Fermi level shifting; established that D-driven response yields helicity-even absorption/gain correction, while G-driven response couples s and p sectors and produces bias-induced circular dichroism with sinθcosθ angular dependence.
AI.conclusion: The combination of specific space group selection and oblique-incidence experimental geometry provides complementary paths for isolating G-driven magnetoelectric electro-optic effects, enabling direct separation of D and G contributions in noncentrosymmetric metals.

title: Tunable Superconductivity Mediated by Heavy-Electron Plasmons: Band-Structure and Quantum-Geometric Engineering
summary: Conventional superconductivity derives its pairing glue from lattice vibrations, tying its characteristic scales to chemistry and atomic masses. Plasmons$-$the collective oscillations of electrons$-$can instead be reshaped through electronic structure engineering, but the principles governing optimal plasmon-mediated pairing remain unclear. Here, we establish such principles for two-carrier systems in which heavy-electron plasmons mediate the pairing of light electrons. Within the random-phase approximation and Eliashberg theory, we calculate the optimal $T_c$ of minimal metallic models and show that it is controlled by a competition between the plasmon energy scale and retardation-driven suppression of the repulsion, yielding optimal carrier densities and band masses. While the plasmon channel alone reaches only $T_c\sim$ 0.1 K, a moderate phonon attraction cooperates with it, boosting $T_c$ by two orders of magnitude to above 20 K. However, the band flattening needed for slow metallic plasmons also favors the development of competing orders. We therefore consider an insulating system in which coherent interband transitions between flat bands generate gapped interband plasmons without free carriers. The heavy-band quantum metric governs the dispersion and electron-plasmon pairing strength of the interband plasmon, while the quantum geometry of the light band suppresses static screening and enhances the net attraction. Because layer separation rapidly weakens pairing, we propose systems with coexisting light and heavy electrons living in different mirror-symmetry sectors of the same layer as promising platforms. Our results establish a new role for flat-band systems in superconductivity: rather than hosting the paired electrons themselves, they can serve as a tunable pairing mediator whose collective charge excitations set the superconducting energy scale beyond their narrow bandwidth.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes principles for plasmon-mediated superconductivity in two-carrier systems, showing that while pure plasmon pairing yields low Tc (~0.1 K), cooperation with phonons boosts Tc to >20 K. It also explores interband plasmons in insulating flat-band systems, where quantum geometry governs pairing, and identifies promising platforms with coexisting light and heavy electrons in the same layer.
AI.motivation: Plasmons (collective electron oscillations) can be engineered via electronic structure, unlike phonons tied to chemistry and atomic masses. However, the principles governing optimal plasmon-mediated pairing were unclear, motivating the need to establish design rules for maximizing Tc via plasmonic pairing.
AI.method: The authors use the random-phase approximation (RPA) and Eliashberg theory to calculate the optimal Tc in minimal metallic models with two-carrier systems (heavy-electron plasmons mediating light-electron pairing). They also analyze insulating flat-band systems with coherent interband transitions generating gapped interband plasmons.
AI.result: Optimal Tc is controlled by competition between plasmon energy scale and retardation-suppressed repulsion. Pure plasmon pairing yields only Tc ~ 0.1 K, but cooperation with moderate phonon attraction boosts Tc to >20 K. In insulators, heavy-band quantum metric governs plasmon dispersion and pairing strength, while light-band quantum geometry suppresses static screening. Layer separation weakens pairing.
AI.conclusion: Flat-band systems can serve as tunable pairing mediators (rather than hosting the paired electrons themselves), with collective charge excitations setting the superconducting energy scale beyond their narrow bandwidth. Systems with coexisting light and heavy electrons in different mirror-symmetry sectors of the same layer are proposed as promising platforms.

title: Period-dependent suppression of Fourier peaks for topography images: Analysis of periodicity of triple-step arrays on vicinal Si(h h m) surfaces
summary: Reliable determination of the periodicity of multiatomic steps on high-Miller-index vicinal surfaces is often complicated by (i) the presence of relatively narrow terraces tilted at large angles relative to the scanning plane, and (ii) unavoidable distortions in the lateral direction resulting from creep and improper calibration of a piezo scanner. We argue that the period of the triple-step arrays on vicinal Si(5\,5\,6) and Si(5 5 7) single-crystal wafers can be determined from raw scanning tunneling microscopy data, without preliminary corrections, with precision approaching the interatomic distance. We demonstrate that the intensity of the Fourier peaks of the differential maps, derived from raw topography images by the difference-of-Gaussians approach, strongly depends on the period of the ordered triple-step arrays. This suppression of the ninth Fourier peak indicates that the regular array of triple steps has a period of $18b=5.99$ nm in projection onto the Si(1 1 1) terrace plane, where $b=0.333$ nm is the distance between atomic rows of the $1\times 1$ lattice in the $[\bar{1}\,\bar{1}\,2]$ direction. This means that the nominally (5\,5\,7)-oriented Si wafers may correspond locally to the Si(8 8 11) orientation. The method can be applied to the precise analysis of other vicinal surfaces with narrow and wide terraces containing an integer number of Si(1 1 1)$7\times 7$ unit cells.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that the periodicity of triple-step arrays on vicinal Si(5 5 6) and Si(5 5 7) surfaces can be accurately determined from raw STM data using a difference-of-Gaussians Fourier analysis, revealing that nominally (5 5 7)-oriented Si may locally correspond to Si(8 8 11) orientation.
AI.motivation: Reliable determination of step periodicity on high-Miller-index vicinal surfaces is hindered by narrow terraces tilted relative to the scanning plane and piezo scanner distortions (creep, calibration errors). A method to extract precise periodicity from raw, uncorrected STM data is needed.
AI.method: Raw STM topography images are processed using a difference-of-Gaussians approach to generate differential maps. Fourier analysis of these maps is performed, and the intensity of Fourier peaks is monitored—specifically, suppression of the ninth Fourier peak indicates a triple-step period of 18b (5.99 nm) projected onto the Si(1 1 1) terrace plane.
AI.result: The ninth Fourier peak suppression reveals the triple-step period is 18b = 5.99 nm (b = 0.333 nm, the atomic row spacing along [\(\bar{1}\bar{1}2\)]). This implies nominally (5 5 7)-oriented Si wafers locally exhibit Si(8 8 11) orientation.
AI.conclusion: The Fourier-based differential mapping method enables precise period determination from raw STM data without corrections, achieving near-interatomic-distance accuracy. It is broadly applicable to vicinal surfaces with stepped terraces containing integer numbers of Si(1 1 1)7×7 unit cells.

title: Tilted Anisotropic Dirac Fermions in an Exponentially Decaying Magnetic Field
summary: We develop an analytical theory of Landau quantization for tilted anisotropic Dirac fermions in an exponentially decaying magnetic field. Using anisotropy scaling and a Lorentz transformation, we recast the laboratory-frame problem into the isotropic Dirac equation in the boosted frame, where the exponentially decaying magnetic-field problem admits an exact solution. Transforming the boosted-frame spectrum back to the laboratory frame yields an implicit quantization condition with an intrinsically energy-dependent guiding-center parameter. We identify the conditions for physically admissible states. We further show that the formalism recovers the known uniform-field spectrum of tilted anisotropic Dirac fermions in the appropriate limit. Our results establish a unified Lorentz-covariant framework for describing Landau quantization in tilted anisotropic Dirac materials in the presence of an exponentially decaying magnetic field.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an analytical theory of Landau quantization for tilted anisotropic Dirac fermions in an exponentially decaying magnetic field, using anisotropy scaling and Lorentz transformation to map the problem to an exactly solvable isotropic Dirac equation in a boosted frame, yielding an implicit quantization condition with an energy-dependent guiding-center parameter.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified analytical framework for Landau quantization in tilted anisotropic Dirac materials under non-uniform (exponentially decaying) magnetic fields, extending beyond the well-studied uniform-field case.
AI.method: The authors use anisotropy scaling and a Lorentz transformation to map the laboratory-frame problem of tilted anisotropic Dirac fermions in an exponentially decaying magnetic field onto an isotropic Dirac equation in a boosted frame, where exact solutions exist. The boosted-frame spectrum is then transformed back to the laboratory frame.
AI.result: An implicit quantization condition with an intrinsically energy-dependent guiding-center parameter is derived. Conditions for physically admissible states are identified, and the formalism recovers the known uniform-field spectrum in the appropriate limit.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a unified Lorentz-covariant framework for describing Landau quantization in tilted anisotropic Dirac materials under exponentially decaying magnetic fields.

title: Nonreciprocal Superconducting Transport from Chiral Edge States
summary: Nonreciprocal superconducting transport enables dissipationless rectification and has attracted considerable interest, yet its microscopic origin is typically sought in bulk electronic states. Here, we show that boundary-controlled chiral edge states in topological systems provide a simple yet largely overlooked mechanism for nonreciprocal superconducting transport. Focusing on chiral kagome antiferromagnets, we demonstrate that out-of-plane spin canting or spin-orbit coupling opens a high-Chern-number bulk gap, giving rise to multiple chiral edge modes. Strikingly, sublattice-dependent boundary termination selects a single-valley character for the edge states, leading to asymmetric edge spectra at opposite edges. This boundary asymmetry directly yields observable nonreciprocal signatures in Josephson junctions oriented transverse to the edges, including asymmetric Andreev spectra, Josephson diode effect, and anomalous Fraunhofer interference patterns. These findings broaden the microscopic understanding of superconducting nonreciprocity and highlight boundary engineering as a tunable route toward superconducting diode devices.

AI.tldr: Boundary-controlled chiral edge states in topological systems, specifically chiral kagome antiferromagnets, provide a mechanism for nonreciprocal superconducting transport, leading to asymmetric Andreev spectra, Josephson diode effect, and anomalous Fraunhofer patterns.
AI.motivation: Nonreciprocal superconducting transport (dissipationless rectification) is of great interest, but its microscopic origin is traditionally attributed to bulk electronic states. The authors identify boundary-controlled chiral edge states as a largely overlooked alternative mechanism.
AI.method: The study focuses on chiral kagome antiferromagnets, where out-of-plane spin canting or spin-orbit coupling opens a high-Chern-number bulk gap, producing multiple chiral edge modes. Sublattice-dependent boundary termination selects a single-valley character for edge states, creating asymmetric edge spectra at opposite edges.
AI.result: Asymmetric edge spectra yield observable nonreciprocal signatures in Josephson junctions oriented transverse to the edges, including asymmetric Andreev spectra, Josephson diode effect, and anomalous Fraunhofer interference patterns.
AI.conclusion: The findings broaden the microscopic understanding of superconducting nonreciprocity and highlight boundary engineering as a tunable route toward superconducting diode devices.

title: Measuring momentum-resolved dissipation of phonon-polaritons in LiNbO$_3$ with terahertz driving
summary: Mapping the dispersion of polaritons, hybrid quasiparticles arising from light-matter coupling, can provide key insights into the material dielectric response, coupling strength, and energy transfer pathways with other excitations. In this work, we present THz pump-Raman probe (TP-RP) as a versatile method for mapping the polariton dispersion in polar non-centrosymmetric materials, demonstrated here for the case of phonon-polaritons in LiNbO$_3$. By resonantly driving polaritonic modes with a broadband THz pump and probing them with a tunable NIR Raman pulse, TP-RP allows for the extraction of the momentum-dependence of both their frequency and damping rate with high accuracy. The spectral features observed in the pump-probe signal, including the polaritonic response as well as pulse artifacts, are reproduced within a many-body theoretical approach. Applying the technique to study the E(TO$_1$) phonon of LiNbO$_3$ enables the combined analysis of theory and experiments to uncover a nontrivial frequency dependence of the phonon intrinsic damping rate, revealing possible anharmonic couplings to other modes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents THz pump-Raman probe (TP-RP) as a versatile method for mapping phonon-polariton dispersion in polar non-centrosymmetric materials, demonstrated on LiNbO₃, revealing momentum-dependent frequency and damping, and uncovering nontrivial frequency dependence of intrinsic phonon damping via combined theory-experiment analysis.
AI.motivation: Mapping polariton dispersion provides key insights into material dielectric response, coupling strength, and energy transfer pathways; existing methods may lack versatility or accuracy, motivating the development of THz pump-Raman probe as a more general approach.
AI.method: THz pump-Raman probe (TP-RP) spectroscopy: broadband THz pump resonantly drives polaritonic modes, while a tunable NIR Raman pulse probes them, enabling extraction of momentum-dependent frequency and damping rate. A many-body theoretical framework reproduces the experimental spectral features.
AI.result: Applied to the E(TO₁) phonon of LiNbO₃, TP-RP accurately extracts the momentum-dependent dispersion and damping rate. Combined theory-experiment analysis uncovers a nontrivial frequency dependence of the intrinsic damping rate, indicating possible anharmonic couplings to other modes.
AI.conclusion: TP-RP is a versatile and accurate method for mapping polariton dispersion in polar non-centrosymmetric materials, and can reveal subtle anharmonic coupling phenomena through detailed analysis of damping behavior.

title: Depth Determination of Individual Shallow NV-Centers via Spin-Lock NMR
summary: Quantitative quantum sensing with shallow electron spins, such as those hosted by nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, requires accurate knowledge of the spin's depth below the host material's surface. A widely used approach infers this depth from the 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) signal of immersion oil on the diamond surface that can be detected using dynamical decoupling sequences such as XY8. However, finite-width pulses make XY8 sensitive to subharmonic responses, including unwanted contributions from nearby 13C spins, and its instrument-limited spectral resolution provides only sparse sampling of the narrow 1H NMR lineshape. Here, we introduce Spin-Lock NMR as an alternative approach to single-NV depth determination. By tuning the Spin-Lock Rabi frequency to the 1H Larmor frequency, the NV probes the 1H NMR signal through the Hartmann-Hahn resonance without the harmonic ambiguities of pulsed decoupling sequences and with substantially higher instrument-limited spectral resolution. We derive a quantitative Spin-Lock NMR fit function from a Markovian master equation that directly relates the measured spectrum to the NV depth. Our approach yields NV depth estimates in excellent agreement with the established XY8-based protocol across multiple NV centers and establishes Spin-Lock NMR as a robust alternative for quantitative single-NV depth determination. To demonstrate its applicability, we employ our method to investigate the 1H nuclear spin signal that is regularly reported to be present on diamond, even in the absence of immersion oil.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Spin-Lock NMR as an alternative to XY8-based protocols for determining the depth of shallow NV centers in diamond. Spin-Lock NMR avoids harmonic ambiguities and offers higher spectral resolution, using a Hartmann-Hahn resonance tuned to the 1H Larmor frequency. The method yields depth estimates consistent with XY8 and is also used to study endogenous 1H signals on diamond surfaces without immersion oil.
AI.motivation: Accurate determination of shallow NV center depth is essential for quantitative quantum sensing. Existing XY8-based depth estimation suffers from subharmonic responses (e.g., from 13C spins) and limited spectral resolution, motivating the need for a more robust alternative.
AI.method: The authors use Spin-Lock NMR, where the Rabi frequency is tuned to the 1H Larmor frequency to probe the NMR signal via the Hartmann-Hahn resonance. A quantitative fit function is derived from a Markovian master equation to directly relate the measured spectrum to NV depth.
AI.result: Spin-Lock NMR yields NV depth estimates in excellent agreement with the XY8 protocol across multiple NV centers. The method also reveals 1H nuclear spin signals present on diamond surfaces even without immersion oil.
AI.conclusion: Spin-Lock NMR is a robust and higher-resolution alternative to pulsed decoupling sequences for single-NV depth determination, avoiding harmonic ambiguities and enabling investigation of intrinsic surface 1H signals.

title: Impurity-induced Inverse Faraday Effect
summary: We provide a quantum-mechanical description of the photoinduced dc current states and magnetic fields around nonmagnetic point impurities in a two-dimensional (2D) electron gas irradiated by a circularly polarized electromagnetic wave. Based on the solution of the corresponding time-dependent Schrodinger equation within the second-order perturbation theory in the electromagnetic wave amplitude we find that the resulting dc magnetic field component perpendicular to the plane of the 2D system is distributed like in a set of random magnetic fluxes bound to the positions of impurities. As a result, the spatially averaged dc magnetic field does not vanish far from the sample edges and, thus, our scenario of the inverse Faraday effect in disordered systems differs strongly from the standard one based on the relaxation time approximation within the hydrodynamic or kinetic equation approaches which would give only the photoinduced currents flowing along the sample edges. The predicted mechanism for formation of rectified currents flowing around the impurity centers is shown to be generic both for 2D and three-dimensional systems. The internal dc magnetic field can give rise to the photoinduced Hall effect and Faraday rotation for a probing electromagnetic signal.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quantum-mechanical analysis of photoinduced DC currents and magnetic fields around nonmagnetic impurities in a 2D electron gas under circularly polarized light, showing that these fields create random magnetic fluxes at impurity sites, leading to a non-vanishing spatially averaged DC magnetic field far from sample edges—contrary to the standard inverse Faraday effect picture.
AI.motivation: To provide a quantum-mechanical description of the inverse Faraday effect in disordered systems, beyond the limitations of the standard relaxation-time approximation in hydrodynamic or kinetic approaches, which only predict photoinduced currents along sample edges.
AI.method: Solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation using second-order perturbation theory in the electromagnetic wave amplitude for a 2D electron gas with nonmagnetic point impurities under circularly polarized radiation.
AI.result: DC magnetic field perpendicular to the 2D plane is distributed like random magnetic fluxes bound to impurities; spatially averaged DC magnetic field does not vanish far from sample edges, differing from the standard inverse Faraday effect scenario; the mechanism is generic for both 2D and 3D systems.
AI.conclusion: The predicted internal DC magnetic field can induce photoinduced Hall effect and Faraday rotation for a probing electromagnetic signal, offering a new understanding of the inverse Faraday effect in disordered systems.

title: Electrical Control of Altermagnetism in a Quasi-1D Magnet
summary: Altermagnetism is a collinear magnetic state characterized by momentum-dependent spin splitting in fully compensated materials. While widely investigated in systems governed by three- or two-dimensional exchange interactions, its extension to quasi-one-dimensional magnets remains almost unexplored. Focusing on the experimentally established AgCrP$_2$S$_6$ van der Waals magnet, we demonstrate that antiferromagnetic chains embedded in a two-dimensional lattice provide a general route to altermagnetism. Combining first-principles calculations and spin-space-group analysis, we show that out-of-plane symmetry breaking can generate a nonrelativistic d-wave spin splitting. An external out-of-plane electric field validates this mechanism, where the induced splitting increases linearly with field strength and reverses sign with field direction. We rationalize such behaviour by constructing an effective tight-binding model, which links the altermagnetic response to anisotropic third-neighbor interchain hoppings. Additionally, we show that Janus substitution also induces a d-wave spin texture, while ferroelectric interfacing with CuInP$_2$S$_6$ enables polarization-controlled spin-split bands in a fully compensated ferrimagnetic state. Our results establish quasi-one-dimensional antiferromagnets as building blocks for altermagnetism.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that quasi-one-dimensional antiferromagnetic chains in a 2D lattice (exemplified by AgCrP₂S₆) can realize altermagnetism with nonrelativistic d-wave spin splitting, controllable via electric fields, Janus substitution, or ferroelectric interfacing.
AI.motivation: While altermagnetism is well-studied in 2D and 3D systems, its realization in quasi-one-dimensional magnets remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: First-principles calculations and spin-space-group analysis are used to study AgCrP₂S₆. An effective tight-binding model is constructed to explain the mechanism, and external electric fields, Janus substitution, and ferroelectric interfacing are employed to validate and control the altermagnetic response.
AI.result: Out-of-plane symmetry breaking generates a nonrelativistic d-wave spin splitting. The splitting scales linearly with applied out-of-plane electric field and reverses sign with field direction. Janus substitution induces similar d-wave texture, and ferroelectric interfacing with CuInP₂S₆ enables polarization-controlled spin splitting in a fully compensated ferrimagnetic state.
AI.conclusion: Quasi-one-dimensional antiferromagnets serve as effective building blocks for realizing altermagnetism, extending the concept beyond 2D/3D systems.

title: Physics-constrained machine learning for decoding multi-nanobubble configurations in graphene
summary: Identifying multiple graphene nanobubbles from electronic spectra is challenging because their strain-induced features overlap. We develop a physics-constrained machine-learning framework that decodes nanobubble configurations from density-of-states (DOS) spectra. For spatially separated nanobubbles, previous full quantum-transport calculations established that the multi-bubble DOS is numerically equivalent to the normalized sum of the constituent single-bubble spectra. We encode this validated additive relation in a compact neural decomposition model. For each target spectrum, the basis coefficients are optimized independently, and the resulting weights directly identify the constituent geometries. The method accurately reconstructs configurations of increasing complexity and remains robust to repeated constituents, incomplete basis dictionaries, and simulated measurement noise. The framework provides an interpretable route for characterizing strain-engineered graphene nanostructures and may extend to other quantum materials with additive spectral responses.

AI.tldr: A physics-constrained machine-learning framework decodes graphene nanobubble configurations from DOS spectra using an additive neural decomposition model, enabling interpretable characterization of strain-engineered nanostructures.
AI.motivation: Identifying multiple graphene nanobubbles from electronic spectra is challenging because their strain-induced features overlap.
AI.method: Physics-constrained machine-learning framework that encodes a validated additive relation (multi-bubble DOS = normalized sum of single-bubble DOS) into a compact neural decomposition model, where basis coefficients are optimized independently to identify constituent geometries.
AI.result: Accurately reconstructs configurations of increasing complexity and remains robust to repeated constituents, incomplete basis dictionaries, and simulated measurement noise.
AI.conclusion: Provides an interpretable route for characterizing strain-engineered graphene nanostructures and may extend to other quantum materials with additive spectral responses.

title: Specimen design for material parameter identification using topology optimization
summary: Constitutive relations close the equations of continuum mechanics, and serve as a surrogate for a material in the design and engineering process. They are often specified in a parameterized form with parameters identified by experiment. In this paper, we propose a framework for identifying experimental configurations that are maximally informative for constitutive model discovery. The framework strongly couples modeling and experimentation: the model leverages high-dimensional data from full-field measurements, while the current uncertainty in the model guides the design of future experiments. We formulate this goal by integrating Bayesian optimal experimental design with topology optimization. The Bayesian design criterion quantifies expected information gain, which drives the topology optimization of the specimen geometry.

AI.tldr: A framework integrating Bayesian optimal experimental design with topology optimization to identify maximally informative experimental configurations for constitutive model discovery.
AI.motivation: Constitutive relations are critical for continuum mechanics but require parameter identification from experiments; existing experimental designs may not be optimally informative for model discovery.
AI.method: Bayesian optimal experimental design is combined with topology optimization; the Bayesian criterion quantifies expected information gain, which drives specimen geometry optimization; full-field measurement data is leveraged.
AI.result: A framework that strongly couples modeling and experimentation, where current model uncertainty guides the design of future experiments via optimized specimen geometries.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables automated design of experiments that are maximally informative for discovering constitutive models by directly optimizing specimen geometry based on information gain.

title: Stripe-Order Altermagnetism
summary: Altermagnetism combines compensated magnetic order with nonrelativistic spin splitting, yet established mechanisms predominantly rely on spin-reversing rotations in Néel-order antiferromagnets. Here we establish stripe-order altermagnetism governed instead by a spin-reversing mirror, placing it outside the usual rotation-based $l$-wave classification. Using two-orbital models, we show that the interplay of stripe spin and orbital orders yields two phases: a stripe altermagnet with mirror-selected nematic spin splitting and a stripe anti-altermagnet with spin-degenerate bands. The latter can support ferroelectric-like electrical control of spin splitting in suitable buckled structures. Random-phase-approximation (RPA) calculations show that stripe-order altermagnetism is favored near half filling under strong hopping anisotropy. The spin-reversing mirror further enforces a purely transverse spin current for an electric field parallel or normal to the mirror plane, providing a direct transport diagnostic.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a new class of altermagnetism based on stripe order and spin-reversing mirror symmetry (rather than rotation-based l-wave classification), identifying two phases (stripe altermagnet and stripe anti-altermagnet) with distinct spin-splitting properties, ferroelectric-like control, and a purely transverse spin current transport signature.
AI.motivation: Existing altermagnetism mechanisms rely on spin-reversing rotations in Néel-order antiferromagnets (l-wave classification). The authors aim to establish stripe-order altermagnetism governed by a spin-reversing mirror, which lies outside the conventional rotation-based framework.
AI.method: Two-orbital models are used to analyze the interplay of stripe spin and orbital orders. Random-phase-approximation (RPA) calculations assess stability near half filling under strong hopping anisotropy.
AI.result: Two phases emerge: a stripe altermagnet (mirror-selected nematic spin splitting) and a stripe anti-altermagnet (spin-degenerate bands). The anti-altermagnet supports ferroelectric-like electrical control of spin splitting in buckled structures. RPA shows stripe-order altermagnetism is favored near half filling with strong hopping anisotropy. The spin-reversing mirror enforces a purely transverse spin current for electric fields parallel or normal to the mirror plane.
AI.conclusion: Stripe-order altermagnetism represents a distinct class beyond rotation-based l-wave altermagnets, with unique spin-splitting control and a direct transport diagnostic via purely transverse spin current.

title: Operando observation of strain relaxation in fatigued pearlitic steel
summary: Pearlitic steels are the material of choice for railway wheels and rails, where their lamellar ferrite-cementite structure balances cost, strength, and wear resistance. However, in use, cyclic loading combined with frictional heat softens the steel, promoting fatigue and eventual failure. Here we use Dark-Field X-ray Microscopy (DFXM) to follow, operando, the grain-scale response of a fatigued pearlitic colony during annealing up to 550 °C. Orientation maps reveal negligible lattice rotation and no sub-cell formation, indicating that the cementite lamellae suppress long-range dislocation motion. Strain maps nonetheless show pronounced relaxation: the elastic strain spread narrows by nearly 40%, with recovery starting below 250 °C, within the operating temperatures of railway wheels. We attribute this relaxation to short-range annihilation of dislocations confined between lamellae, linking grain-scale strain recovery to the macroscopic softening of pearlitic railway steels in service.

AI.tldr: Using Dark-Field X-ray Microscopy (DFXM), this study reveals that during annealing up to 550°C, pearlitic steel's cementite lamellae suppress long-range dislocation motion but allow short-range dislocation annihilation, causing elastic strain relaxation by ~40% starting below 250°C—linking grain-scale recovery to macroscopic softening in railway wheels.
AI.motivation: Pearlitic steels are widely used for railway wheels and rails due to their balance of cost, strength, and wear resistance, but cyclic loading and frictional heat cause softening that promotes fatigue and failure. Understanding the grain-scale mechanisms of this softening is critical for improving rail steel performance.
AI.method: The authors used operando Dark-Field X-ray Microscopy (DFXM) to follow the grain-scale response of a fatigued pearlitic colony during annealing up to 550°C, capturing orientation and strain maps.
AI.result: Orientation maps showed negligible lattice rotation and no sub-cell formation, indicating cementite lamellae suppress long-range dislocation motion. Strain maps revealed pronounced relaxation: elastic strain spread narrowed by ~40%, with recovery starting below 250°C.
AI.conclusion: The relaxation is attributed to short-range annihilation of dislocations confined between lamellae, directly linking grain-scale strain recovery to the macroscopic softening of pearlitic railway steels in service.

title: Resonant excitations via low frequency pumping in driven magnon systems
summary: We analyse resonant excitations of ferromagnetic magnons via microwave pumping using Floquet theory. Special focus is put on driving frequencies that are below the corresponding magnon energy, which can be excited in large parameter regions via parametric resonances. We develop a theoretical framework that analytically predicts the regions of resonances and resonance thresholds in thin films of ferro- and ferri-magnetic materials like YIG as a function of damping, amplitude and frequency. Resonance regions are separated by exceptional points of the quasi-energies and the results are compared with micromagnetic simulations. The corresponding threshold amplitudes can be estimated from a characteristic powerlaw with damping, leading to the possibility of targeted exciatations at selected wavenumbers using low frequency drive.

AI.tldr: This paper uses Floquet theory to analyze resonant microwave pumping of ferromagnetic magnons, showing that sub-frequency magnons can be excited via parametric resonances, with analytical predictions for resonance regions and thresholds in thin magnetic films like YIG.
AI.motivation: To enable targeted excitation of magnons at selected wavenumbers using low-frequency microwave pumping, overcoming the conventional energy-matching constraint.
AI.method: Floquet theory analysis of parametric resonances in ferromagnetic thin films, with analytical prediction of resonance regions and thresholds, validated by micromagnetic simulations and characterized by exceptional points of quasi-energies.
AI.result: Resonance regions separated by exceptional points; threshold amplitudes follow a characteristic power law with damping; sub-frequency magnon excitations achievable in large parameter regions.
AI.conclusion: Low-frequency driving can selectively excite magnons at specific wavenumbers, enabling new control paradigms for magnonic devices.

title: Contrasting $Γ$- and K-Valley Moiré Physics in Twisted Monolayer/Bilayer WSe$_2$
summary: Electronic orbital character plays a central role in determining electronic correlations, spin-orbit coupling, dimensionality, and ultimately the quantum phases of condensed-matter systems. Two-dimensional moiré materials have emerged as highly tunable platforms for exploring correlated phenomena, but the role of orbital degrees of freedom remains largely unexplored. Here, we identify twisted monolayer/bilayer WSe$_2$ as a platform in which displacement-field tuning enables moiré physics to be realized in both the $K$ and $Γ$ valleys. The distinct orbital characters of these valleys give rise to contrasting correlated phases at moiré filling factors $ν=1$ and $ν=1/3$. At $ν=1$, the $K$-valley state is a weak insulator, consistent with an antiferromagnetic state near a van Hove singularity in the intermediate-coupling regime, similar to that observed in twisted bilayer WSe$_2$. In contrast, the $Γ$-valley state exhibits a pronounced Pomeranchuk effect, consistent with proximity to a Mott transition. At $ν=1/3$, the $K$ valley hosts a robust generalized Wigner crystal, whereas the $Γ$-valley state lies near the crystallization boundary and again exhibits a Pomeranchuk effect, with localization enhanced by increasing temperature or magnetic field. Our work highlights the importance of orbital character in defining quantum phases in moiré systems, and identify the $Γ$ valley as a promising platform for exploring correlated phenomena near quantum phase transitions, where competing phases and enhanced fluctuations may give rise to unconventional phases.
